🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: The "old edge" was the perimeter firewall; the "new edge" is wherever identity + Internet meet. This is why zero-trust architecture and endpoint EDR/XDR displaced perimeter-only defense.

front: 🔍 What is passive discovery in attack-surface management, and what does it reveal?
back:
Passive discovery describes methods used to indirectly identify systems, services, and protocols — leveraging careful observation rather than active probing.

Primary technique: network packet capture.

What it reveals:
• Network-connected hosts
• Communications channels
• Protocols in use
• Activity patterns

💡 Contrast with active discovery (ICMP/TCP/UDP scans, Nmap, service probes): passive is quieter and less likely to be noticed by adversaries or to trigger IDS/IPS. But it only sees what actually generates traffic during observation.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Passive discovery is often the only option in OT/ICS environments where active scanning can crash legacy PLCs. Tools like Zeek, Wireshark, and NetFlow collectors are staples.

front: 🚨 What is an Indicator of Compromise (IoC)?
back:
An Indicator of Compromise (IoC) is a suspicious behavior, pattern, or artifact that suggests malicious activity is occurring — a clue that helps the analyst detect a threat.

Analogy from CertMaster: security analysts are the detectives of the network. Recognizing unusual patterns is the first line of defense — the more familiar you are with normal behavior, the faster you catch abnormal.

⚠️ Terminology depth (comes back in Module 10):
• Atomic IoCs — single-value artifacts (IPs, domains, file hashes)
• Behavioral IoCs — patterns of activity (impossible travel, data staging)
• IoC vs IoA — an Indicator of Attack shows an attack in progress; an IoC often shows a compromise that already happened

front: 🚨 CertMaster names three categories of network Indicators of Compromise. Name each and describe what to watch for.
back:
1. Rogue Devices — any unauthorized device on the network (computers, phones, wireless routers, or specialized hardware). Example: a hidden Raspberry Pi forwarding traffic to an attacker.

2. Enumeration Activities — an attacker probing for information on devices, systems, users, and processes. Causes a spike in network traffic as the probe systematically walks the network.

3. Anomalous Activity — anything outside the normal baseline. Examples: large data transfers outside business hours, multiple attempted failed logins, spikes in traffic from unusual sources.

💡 Recognizing these before the attack proper is huge — enumeration precedes exploitation, so catching it early can stop the incident before it starts.

front: 🌐 What are the four attacker techniques CertMaster lists for exploiting unexpected network ports?
back:
1. Port Hopping — quickly switching between ports to send traffic through, evading rules that pin monitoring to specific ports

2. Port Masquerading — sending malicious traffic through a legitimate port so it blends in. Example: malware opening a secure shell on port 22 so it looks like normal SSH.

3. Tunneling — wrapping one protocol inside another. Example: hiding FTP traffic inside DNS queries (port 53) to exfiltrate data through DNS tunneling.

4. Using High-Numbered Ports — ports above 1024 are often less closely monitored

💡 Detection tools called out by CertMaster: IDS, firewalls, and network logs. Baselines of "expected port behavior per host role" are what make these detections tractable.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: DNS tunneling (exfil over port 53) is one of the most persistent covert-channel techniques. DNS-inspection tools and NextGen firewalls flag anomalously long or high-entropy DNS queries.

front: 🌐 Give the port-to-protocol mappings CertMaster uses in the "activity on unexpected ports" section.
back:
• Port 21 → FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
• Port 22 → SSH (Secure Shell) — port-masquerading example: malware opens SSH here to blend in
• Port 53 → DNS — tunneling example: exfiltrating data inside DNS queries
• Port 80 → HTTP

💡 CertMaster's canonical unexpected-port scenario: a web server that has no FTP role starts receiving traffic on port 21. That's unexpected and warrants immediate investigation.

⚠️ For the exam, memorize the common port set: 20/21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP.

front: 🔍 What is a discovery scan, and how does it relate to a baseline?
back:
A discovery scan quickly surveys the network to identify all devices/systems actually connected, along with active IP addresses, hostnames, and basic information.

Characteristics:
• Quick and lightweight — doesn't slow the network
• Performed at regular intervals, not one-time
• Should be run any time the network changes (new devices added)

💡 Discovery scans build the baseline of authorized devices. Once you know what's supposed to be there, spotting unauthorized devices becomes much easier.

⚠️ Distinguish from a vulnerability scan (later modules): discovery finds what's there, vulnerability scan finds what's wrong with what's there.

front: 🔍 CertMaster lists seven types of discovery scans. Name each and give a one-line characterization.
back:
1. ICMP / Ping — most common; sends ICMP packets to every IP in the range
2. TCP SYN Scan — used when ICMP is blocked; sends TCP SYN to a port; SYN-ACK reply = device active
3. UDP Scans — sends UDP packets to common UDP ports (e.g., 53 DNS); response or "port unreachable" error confirms presence
4. ARP Scans — ARP request on local subnet; device with the IP replies even if it ignored other scans. Very noisy on the local subnet.
5. Service Probes — sends a valid protocol request (e.g., HTTP GET on port 80)
6. DNS Zone Transfers — queries internal DNS servers; can reveal hostnames and IPs for local systems
7. SNMP Sweeps — queries devices using known SNMP community strings

💡 When ICMP fails, ARP-scan on the local subnet is often the highest-yield fallback (arp-scan / Nmap -PR) — but its noise makes it obvious to a monitoring IDS.

⚠️ Zone-transfer discovery relies on misconfigured DNS. Correctly configured DNS restricts zone transfers to authorized secondaries — Lesson 3A explicitly cites this as a common mitigation.

front: 🔍 Compare Nmap and Angry IP Scanner.
back:
• Nmap — open-source, multi-platform, CLI (with Zenmap GUI). Diverse scans: find live hosts, open ports, service/version identification, OS detection, scriptable via NSE.

• Angry IP Scanner — GUI-based, fast multi-threaded. Basic ping scan for host discovery plus selected port scans; returns hostname and MAC. Ideal for asset inventory and basic discovery.

💡 Rule of thumb: reach for Angry IP for a fast asset inventory; reach for Nmap when you need depth (service/version, OS, scripted checks).

⚠️ Both tools are also used by attackers and red teams — traffic that looks like Nmap or Angry IP could be malicious reconnaissance, not just your own scans.

front: 🔍 What can Nmap discover about a target?
back:
Nmap can identify:
• Live hosts (host discovery)
• Open ports
• Services and their versions running on those ports
• The operating system the device is running (OS fingerprinting)

Plus, via the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE):
• Presence of known vulnerabilities
• Misconfigured services
• Weak authentication settings
• Outdated, vulnerable software

💡 Nmap has a GUI version called Zenmap that performs all the same functions.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: NSE elevates Nmap from a scanner into a lightweight vulnerability assessment tool. It's frequently the first thing an analyst reaches for during external attack-surface review.

front:
🔍 Nmap flag reference — give the meaning of each flag CertMaster covers:

-sS   -sU   -sn   -PR   -sV   -p   -p-   -O   -T4
back:
• -sS — TCP SYN scan ("half-open" / stealth scan; less likely to be logged)
• -sU — UDP scan (sends packets to common UDP ports)
• -sn — Host discovery only (disables port scans; identifies live hosts)
• -PR — ARP ping for host discovery on local subnet
• -sV — Service/version detection on open ports
• -p — Port range (specify individual ports or ranges)
• -p- — Scan all 65,535 ports
• -O — OS detection (fingerprint the target OS)
• -T4 — Timing template "Aggressive" (speeds up the scan; balances speed and accuracy)

💡 Timing templates run T0–T5: T0 paranoid (very slow, IDS-evading), T3 default, T4 aggressive, T5 insane (fastest, may be inaccurate). CertMaster covers T4 explicitly.

⚠️ Exam favorite: distinguishing -sS (SYN scan — never completes handshake, low logging) from -sT (TCP connect scan — full handshake, higher logging).

front:
🔍 Interpret this Nmap command and explain what each option does:

nmap -sS -T4 -O -sV -p- 192.168.50.9
back:
This command performs a comprehensive scan of a single host: 192.168.50.9.

• -sS — stealthy SYN scan (half-open; less likely to be logged)
• -T4 — Aggressive timing (speeds up scan; balances speed and accuracy)
• -O — attempts OS identification of each host
• -sV — probes open ports to determine service and version
• -p- — scans all 65,535 ports
• 192.168.50.9 — the target IP

⚠️ CertMaster explicitly warns this scan is invasive and slow: the example took ~100 seconds against a single host and generates significant network traffic. Scanning multiple IPs this way would take a very long time.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: This flag combination — SYN + OS detect + service versioning + all ports — is a hallmark of a thorough reconnaissance scan. If you see traffic that matches this pattern originating from a non-scanning host, treat it as suspect.

front:
🔍 Interpret this Nmap output:

Starting Nmap 7.98 ( https://nmap.org ) at 2025-09-03 14:18 -0400
Nmap scan report for 192.168.50.9
Host is up (0.0084s latency).
Not shown: 65531 closed tcp ports (reset)
PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION
1400/tcp open upnp
1410/tcp open tcpwrapped
1443/tcp open ssl/upnp
1843/tcp open ssl/netopia-vo5?
MAC Address: C4:38:75:17:2E:AF (Sonos)
Device type: general purpose
Running: Linux 3.X|4.X
OS details: Linux 3.2 - 4.14
back:
The scan reports a live host with four open TCP ports, all in the 1400–1843 range. Interpretation:

• Host is up — target responded; latency 8.4 ms
• Not shown: 65531 closed tcp ports (reset) — of 65,535 scanned, all others responded with RST (closed)
• Four open ports, all running UPnP or UPnP-adjacent services (three are UPnP/ssl-UPnP; port 1843 is questionable — "?" indicates uncertain service ID)
• MAC: C4:38:75:17:2E:AF (Sonos) — vendor OUI identifies the device as a Sonos device
• OS: Linux kernel 3.2–4.14 (Sonos speakers run Linux)

💡 Key takeaway for the exam: Nmap output identifies host state, port state per port, service and version, MAC-address vendor, and OS fingerprint — all from one scan. Read each column methodically.

⚠️ The "?" after a service name means Nmap could not confidently identify it — it's a best guess based on partial fingerprint match.

front: 🔍 What is the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE), and what does it enable beyond simple port scanning?
back:
The NSE is Nmap's built-in script-scanning functionality. It lets you use built-in scripts, community/user-made scripts, or create your own.

What NSE detects beyond ports and services:
• Outdated, vulnerable software
• Misconfigured services
• Weak authentication settings
• Presence of specific known vulnerabilities (CVEs)

💡 Common categories: auth, vuln, exploit, discovery, safe, intrusive. Called with --script or -sC (default scripts).

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: NSE turns Nmap into a lightweight vulnerability scanner. It doesn't replace Nessus/OpenVAS/Qualys, but it's the fastest tool for a targeted check like "is this SMB server vulnerable to EternalBlue?"

front: 🔍 CertMaster lists six Nmap port states. Name all six with a one-line definition.
back:
Determinate states (regular TCP scans):
• Open — an application on the host is accepting connections
• Closed — the port responds with an RST packet; port is reachable but no application is listening
• Filtered — Nmap cannot probe the port; usually a firewall is silently discarding the probes

Indeterminate states (unable to reliably determine):
• Unfiltered — Nmap can probe but cannot tell open from closed; used with ACK scan to test firewall rulesets
• Open|Filtered — reported by UDP and IP protocol scans when open cannot be distinguished from filtered
• Closed|Filtered — reported by TCP Idle scans that cannot distinguish closed from filtered

⚠️ Exam trap: Closed ≠ Filtered. Closed means the port is reachable but has no listener (RST replied). Filtered means the port is behind a device dropping the probes — you don't even know if a listener exists.

front: 🔍 An Nmap scan reports a port as Filtered. What does that indicate, and how does it differ from Closed?
back:
• Filtered — Nmap cannot probe the port because a firewall (or similar packet filter) is silently discarding the probes. You get no answer at all.

• Closed — the port responds with an RST packet. It's reachable, but no application is listening. You know the host exists and the port is not filtered.

💡 Diagnostic value: filtered ports tell you where firewalls are dropping traffic; closed ports tell you what listeners aren't running but could be. Filtered = enforced silence; Closed = reachable but empty.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: An entire host reporting all ports as "filtered" often means a firewall is silently blocking all probes — the host might not exist at all. Combine with an ARP scan on the local subnet to disambiguate.

front: 🚨 What is active exploitation, and what important distinction does CertMaster call out about the term?
back:
Active exploitation refers to vulnerabilities that attackers have already taken advantage of — not potential vulnerabilities.

Critical CertMaster distinction: active exploitation does NOT refer to an "active attack" currently in progress. It refers to whether the vulnerability itself is being exploited in the wild.

💡 Why the distinction matters: an actively-exploited vulnerability jumps to the top of the remediation queue regardless of the CVSS score, because working exploits exist and attackers are using them.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: This concept overlaps with CISA's KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) Catalog and EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) score. Both answer the same question: "is anyone actually using this vuln right now?"

front: 🧠 Define threat intelligence and list the main sources CertMaster names.
back:
Threat intelligence is all the information and insights that have been gathered, analyzed, and interpreted to identify potential threats and vulnerabilities — including the latest TTPs, hacker group activity, and actively exploited vulnerabilities.

Sources:
• Vendor alerts (Microsoft, Cisco, etc.)
• Government agencies (CISA, FBI, NSA)
• Public threat feeds
• Commercial threat intelligence providers

Sharing mechanisms: ISACs, cybersecurity groups, conferences, online forums, law-enforcement coordination, and threat-intelligence platforms.

💡 CertMaster's "weather forecast" analogy: threat intel doesn't stop the storm, but it tells you what's coming so you can prepare.

front: 🧠 What is an ISAC, and what role does it play in threat intelligence?
back:
ISAC — Information Sharing and Analysis Center. Industry-specific member groups that share threat information among peer organizations (financial-services ISAC, healthcare ISAC, IT-ISAC, etc.).

Role:
• Distribute IoCs, TTPs, and active-threat data among peers
• Enable industry-wide response (a threat hitting one bank often hits all banks)
• Bridge private-sector intel with government reporting

💡 CertMaster's key claim: participation in an ISAC or similar industry group dramatically reduces the time analysts spend on threat detection — because peers surface novel threats first, and the community collectively identifies indicators faster than any one team could.

🔗 Related: the Cyber Threat Alliance (CTA) is a similar sharing group — many leading cybersecurity vendors share threat information through it.

front: 🧠 What is CISA's Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) program?
back:
AIS is a US CISA-managed program that lets groups quickly exchange threat information in a machine-readable format.

Value:
• Automates threat-intel exchange (no manual copy/paste)
• Enables computers to consume indicators directly
• Helps organizations "stop attackers from using the same tricks repeatedly"

💡 AIS uses standardized formats — notably STIX (data) and TAXII (transport) — so different tools can consume the same feeds without translation.

🔗 Related agency-driven feeds: FBI FLASH alerts, NSA Cybersecurity Advisories, NCSC advisories in allied countries.

front: 🧠 Distinguish STIX from TAXII — what each stands for and its role.
back:
• STIX — Structured Threat Information eXpression. The data format / language that describes threat information (indicators, TTPs, threat actors, incidents). STIX is what you send.

• TAXII — Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information. The message-exchange / transport protocol used to share STIX-formatted data between systems. TAXII is how you send it.

💡 Analogy: STIX is the letter; TAXII is the postal service. You could hand-deliver STIX (email, GitHub) but TAXII automates the delivery over standard servers.

⚠️ Exam trap: they're almost always tested as a pair, but they answer different questions. If a question is about data structure → STIX. If about real-time exchange → TAXII.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Threat intel platforms (MISP, ThreatConnect, Anomali) speak STIX/TAXII natively so IOC feeds from CISA, ISACs, and commercial providers can be ingested automatically.

front: 🧠 What is MISP?
back:
MISP — Malware Information Sharing Platform. An open-source threat-intel platform used to gather, analyze, and share threat information across teams and organizations.

CertMaster note: MISP uses standardized taxonomies to support confidence assessment — including estimative language and the Admiralty Scale.

💡 MISP is a common choice for orgs building their own threat-intel program because it's free, integrates with STIX/TAXII feeds, and supports both automated indicator exchange and manual analyst workflow.

front: 🧠 What questions does a threat intelligence analyst ask when assigning a confidence level to intel?
back:
• How likely is this information to be accurate?
• Is the source trustworthy?
• Do multiple sources corroborate the evidence?

After answering these, the analyst assigns a confidence level. This filters out noise and helps the team focus on the most significant threats rather than false positives.

💡 The three most common taxonomies for expressing confidence: the Admiralty Scale (2-axis grade), estimative language (probability phrasing), and platform-specific scores (e.g., MISP's built-in).

front: 🧠 Describe the Admiralty Scale — both axes and what a grade like "A1" means.
back:
The Admiralty Scale is a two-axis framework that grades both the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information.

Source reliability — letter scale A through F:
• A — completely reliable
• E — completely unreliable
• F — new source; reliability cannot be judged

Information credibility — number scale 1 through 6:
• 1 — confirmed by multiple sources
• 5 — unconfirmed
• 6 — credibility cannot be judged

Combined example: A1 = information confirmed by multiple sources from a completely reliable source. Highest-confidence grade.



⚠️ Exam trap: F (source) and 6 (info) both mean "cannot be judged" — not "unreliable/unconfirmed" (which would be E and 5). Watch for stems that describe a "new, unproven source" and mislabel it as unreliable.

front: 🧠 What is the estimative language framework, and give the CertMaster-listed probability ranges.
back:
Estimative language provides clear standardized wording to express levels of certainty or uncertainty, paired with probability percentages. Used in reports and alerts so readers can quickly interpret the confidence level.

Common phrases (per CertMaster):
• Highly likely — 80–99% probability
• Even chance — 40–60% probability
• Unlikely — 20–40% probability

💡 Full estimative-language ladder in most frameworks (e.g., ODNI): Almost No Chance → Very Unlikely → Unlikely → Roughly Even Chance → Likely → Very Likely → Almost Certain.

⚠️ Exam trap: "even chance" (40–60%) is not "unlikely" (20–40%) — the phrases don't overlap. Read percentages carefully.

front: 🚦 What is a vulnerability prioritization matrix, and what two axes does CertMaster's example use?
back:
A prioritization matrix compares two values to determine a vulnerability's priority level. CertMaster's example matrix compares:

• Impact Value (Y axis) — Low (1), Med (5), High (10)
• Threat Likelihood (X axis) — Low (1), Med (5), High (10)

Cell values are the products: Low/Low = 1, top-right High/High = 100, off-diagonal medium/high or high/medium = 50.

💡 Key insight from CertMaster: a vulnerability may be highly prioritized even if likelihood is only moderate, as long as the potential impact is high. High-impact × moderate-likelihood still lands in the top tier.

🔗 This is the qualitative version of quantitative risk analysis — you'll see the same probability × impact structure in Security+ and in risk-management coursework.

front: 🚦 CertMaster lists five common criteria for prioritizing vulnerabilities. Name all five.
back:
1. Risk Appetite — the organization's tolerance level determines which risks need to be addressed first
2. Active Exploitation — if the vuln is being actively exploited, address it immediately
3. Asset Value — a vuln on a server hosting customer data outranks the same vuln on a test server
4. Impact — potential consequences of the vulnerability being exploited
5. Patch Availability — if a patch is available, the vuln can be resolved quickly

💡 Rule of thumb: active exploitation trumps everything else. If a critical vulnerability is being exploited in the wild right now, patch availability is the only other question that matters.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: In practice, orgs also fold in EPSS score (exploit probability), CVSS environmental metrics (asset context), and threat intel about targeted-vs-opportunistic exploitation.

front: 🛡️ CertMaster lists five mitigation strategies after asset inventory. Name each with a one-line description.
back:
1. Access Control — strict controls like MFA; limits access to sensitive data
2. Patching and Updating — automated patch management to prevent exploitation of known vulns
3. Network Segmentation — split large networks into smaller subnets to contain breaches
4. Removing Unnecessary Components — every removed component is a pathway an attacker cannot exploit
5. Employee Training — awareness of risks and how to recognize and report threats

💡 Asset inventory comes first — before applying any of these, you must identify all hardware/software assets and user accounts to determine which are essential and which can be removed.

⚠️ Strategies can be used concurrently. CertMaster's DNS zone-transfer example applies both access control and network segmentation.

front: 🛡️ CertMaster's IIS banner example: a web server running Microsoft IIS reveals its exact version in HTTP response headers. What mitigation strategy is used, and why?
back:
✅ Removing Unnecessary Components (or "reducing exposure").

Action: disable IIS banner broadcasting so the version string is not returned in response headers.

Why it matters: version-disclosure banners hand an attacker a direct match to CVE lookups. Knowing "IIS 8.5" enables the attacker to check exploit-DB and Metasploit for that exact version and skip the enumeration step entirely.

💡 Same principle applies broadly:
• Apache ServerTokens Prod
• SSH banner rewriting
• SMTP EHLO banner customization

⚠️ This mitigates reconnaissance, not exploitation — it doesn't fix a vulnerable IIS install, it just makes discovery slower. Still valuable because it shifts opportunistic attackers to easier targets.

front: 🛡️ You discover the public DNS server allows zone transfers. Why is this a vulnerability, and how do you mitigate it?
back:
Vulnerability: an attacker performing a DNS zone transfer can obtain a list of internal hostnames and IP addresses — a full reconnaissance dump of the internal DNS namespace.

Mitigation:
• Disable unauthorized zone transfers
• Ensure only authorized secondary DNS servers can request them

💡 CertMaster explicitly frames this as an example of applying both access control and network segmentation concurrently — one control alone doesn't fully address it.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: dig AXFR example.com @ns.example.com is the classic zone-transfer command. External red teams and pentest reports frequently flag this as an easy finding when internal DNS is exposed.

front: 🪤 CertMaster's honeypot example: the security team deploys a honeypot mimicking a vulnerable database. After a few days, external IPs attempt to exploit it. What is done with this data?
back:
The team updates firewall and IDS rules to block similar traffic that might be targeting real assets.

CertMaster identifies this as an example of two mitigation strategies applied together:
• Asset inventory — knowing which devices are real and which are the honeypot
• Employee training — using the gathered data for analysis and awareness

💡 Honeypots are covered further in Module 6 (cyber deception). Their value is producing high-fidelity IoCs — because no legitimate user should ever touch a honeypot, any traffic to it is malicious by definition.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: The tradeoff with honeypots is maintenance overhead. Modern approaches include lightweight "honeytokens" (fake credentials, canary files) that scale better than full-service honeypots.

front: 🛡️ Define system hardening.
back:
System hardening is the process of making a system as secure as possible while still remaining usable.

CertMaster explicitly names this as the primary job in cybersecurity.

Rationale: new devices ship with many defaults optimized for ease of setup and broad compatibility, not for security. Out of the box, they typically have a lot of vulnerabilities — unnecessary services running, default credentials, permissive settings.

💡 Hardening is inherently a tradeoff. The most secure device is one turned off in a Faraday cage — but it's also useless. The analyst's job is to find the point where security and usability meet the organization's risk appetite.

front: 🛡️ CertMaster names seven common hardening steps that apply to nearly any system. List them.
back:
1. Remove unnecessary software and services — evaluate each system's role; anything not needed is uninstalled or disabled (e.g., a web server doesn't need a print service)
2. Apply security updates and patches — test then apply vendor patches
3. Change default settings — especially default usernames/passwords
4. Disable unused network ports and protocols — close unused ports; disable insecure protocols like Telnet
5. Enable and configure firewalls — host-based (software) or network-based (hardware)
6. Strong authentication and access controls — implement principle of least privilege and strong password policies

💡 CertMaster's explicit callout for insecure protocols to disable: Telnet. Its modern replacement is SSH (Secure Shell). Other legacy protocols to disable when possible: FTP (use SFTP/FTPS), unencrypted SMB v1, RSH/rlogin.

front: 🔑 Summarize the NIST 2024 password policy guidelines as described by CertMaster and describe how they diverge from pre-2017 guidance.
back:
Length — the primary factor:
• Minimum 8 characters
• NIST guidelines recommend 15 or more characters
• Focus on longer passphrases rather than complex short passwords

Complexity — de-emphasized:
• Mixed case, numbers, and specials are still a good idea
• Forcing complexity often produces predictable patterns like C0mpTIA@
• Complexity does not make a significant difference in crack time; length is the primary determining factor

Password resets:
• Do NOT reset on a regular interval (e.g., every 90 days)
• Reset only on evidence of potential compromise
• Interval-based resets lead to insecure, incrementally modified passwords

MFA: use TOTP or hardware security keys; avoid SMS-based MFA

Password managers: NIST recommends users employ password managers to keep passwords unique per site

⚠️ Exam-worthy shift: the "90-day password rotation" that dominated pre-2017 policy is explicitly discouraged under current NIST guidance. If a stem describes forced rotation as best practice, that's a distractor.

front: 🔑 CertMaster shows that CompTIA25! and comptia251 both take ~12 days to crack, but the passphrase I am CySA+ certified takes ~50,000 years. What does this illustrate?
back:
Length dominates crack time far more than complexity.

• CompTIA25! — 10 chars with complexity → ~12 days
• comptia251 — 10 chars, no complexity → also ~12 days
• I am CySA+ certified — 20 chars as a passphrase → ~50,000 years
• i am cysa+ certified — same length, no case complexity → same ~50,000 years

💡 Takeaway: a memorable 20-character passphrase beats a difficult-to-type 10-character password by orders of magnitude — and it's easier for the user to remember, reducing pressure to reuse or write it down.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: This is the underlying math behind the xkcd "correct horse battery staple" cartoon — and it's why NIST's 2017-onward guidance shifted from complexity to length.

front:
💻 Match each mainstream OS to its default file system:

A) Windows
B) Linux
C) macOS
back:
A) Windows → NTFS (New Technology File System)
B) Linux → ext4 (Fourth Extended Filesystem)
C) macOS → APFS (Apple File System)

💡 All three are hierarchical (tree-structured) with a root directory holding folders and files.

Historical context (not on exam but useful):
• Windows also supports FAT32, exFAT, ReFS
• Linux common alternatives: XFS, Btrfs, ZFS, F2FS
• macOS pre-2017 used HFS+ (Mac OS Extended)

front: 💻 What is an NTFS Alternate Data Stream (ADS), and why does it matter to a security analyst?
back:
An ADS is an NTFS feature that allows a file to contain more than one stream of data. The main stream is the file's visible contents; additional streams can be added without altering the file's visible size or attributes.

Original purpose: compatibility with Apple's file system (Macintosh resource forks). Also used legitimately by backup programs for temporary snapshots.

Security concern: attackers exploit ADS to hide malware inside a legitimate file. The malware attached to a benign-looking file's alternate stream is very difficult to detect by antimalware scanners.

💡 CLI syntax: legit.txt:evil.exe — the colon after the filename opens a named stream. dir /r reveals ADS in modern Windows. Sysinternals streams.exe is the classic detection tool.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: ADS abuse is a T1564.004 MITRE ATT&CK technique (Hide Artifacts: NTFS File Attributes). EDR products flag it; standalone AV often does not.

front: 💻 Name the four critical folders at the root of a Windows C: drive and what each contains.
back:
• C:\Windows — core OS files; contains boot files and the System32 folder (drivers, registry hives, system libraries, core executables)

• C:\Users — local profile data for all users on the machine

• C:\Program Files — installed 64-bit applications

• C:\Program Files (x86) — installed 32-bit applications

💡 On a 64-bit Windows, both Program Files folders exist. On a 32-bit Windows, only C:\Program Files exists.

⚠️ Exam trap: 64-bit apps live in Program Files; 32-bit apps live in Program Files (x86). The "(x86)" name refers to the 32-bit x86 instruction set — counterintuitive, but that's how Microsoft named it.

front: 💻 What are the key subpaths under C:\Windows and what do they hold?
back:
• C:\Windows\System32 — vital executables, DLL libraries, and configuration files that Windows needs to boot and operate

• C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs — Event and security logs (Windows Event Log .evtx files live here)

• C:\Windows\System32\Config — hive files for the Windows registry (SYSTEM, SECURITY, SOFTWARE, SAM, DEFAULT)

⚠️ Exam favorite: where are Windows event logs stored? → C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs. Common log files: Security.evtx, System.evtx, Application.evtx.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: In IR, System32 changes are always red flags. Attackers use it as a hiding spot because analysts skip past its "expected" contents. Tools like Autoruns and Sysinternals rootkit detectors compare against known-good baselines.

front:
💻 Identify the role of each key Windows system file:

bootmgr  winload.exe  ntoskrnl.exe  winlogon.exe  explorer.exe
back:
• bootmgr — Windows boot manager (loads the OS selection screen if multiple installed)
• winload.exe — Windows boot loader (loads the kernel)
• ntoskrnl.exe — the Windows kernel, the core component / brain of the OS
• winlogon.exe — manages user logons (secure attention sequence, Ctrl-Alt-Del)
• explorer.exe — provides and manages the GUI and desktop interface (taskbar, Start menu, File Explorer)

💡 Boot sequence: bootmgr → winload.exe → ntoskrnl.exe → session manager → winlogon.exe → user shell (explorer.exe).

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Malware masquerading as explorer.exe or winlogon.exe is a classic host indicator — but only when running from a wrong path (e.g., C:\Users\Public\explorer.exe instead of System32).

front: 💻 What is the Windows Registry?
back:
The Windows Registry is a hierarchical database for storing operating system, device, and software application configuration information.

It is comprised of five root keys that contain computer and user databases:
• HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM)
• HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU)
• HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT (HKCR)
• HKEY_USERS (HKU)
• HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG (HKCC)

💡 Registry queries are so central to Windows troubleshooting and forensics that CySA+ expects familiarity with the root-key structure and the on-disk hive files that back them.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Persistence-mechanism registry keys (Run, RunOnce, services) are prime targets for IR. Tools like Autoruns, Registry Explorer, and volatility parse them.

front: 💻 Name the five Windows Registry root keys and describe what each contains.
back:
• HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM) — configuration settings common to all users on the computer (hardware and software)

• HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU) — settings for the currently logged-in user (desktop preferences, user-specific app configs)

• HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT (HKCR) — file associations and how Windows should open files of different types

• HKEY_USERS (HKU) — holds subkeys for each user profile loaded on the system

• HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG (HKCC) — information gathered at startup about the current hardware configuration

💡 HKCU is actually a "shortcut" into HKU\. HKCR is a merged view of HKLM\Software\Classes and HKCU\Software\Classes.

⚠️ Exam trap: HKLM is machine-wide, HKCU is per-user. Malware persistence keys like Run exist in both — the difference is who executes them (all users vs. just one).

front: 💻 What are Windows Registry hive files, and where are they stored?
back:
The registry database is stored in binary files called hives. A hive comprises:
• A single file (no extension) — the hive data itself
• A .LOG file — transaction log
• A .SAV file — copy of the key as it was at the end of setup
• (SYSTEM hive also has a .ALT backup file)

Location: most hive files are in C:\Windows\System32\Config. The exception is NTUSER.DAT, which is stored in each user's profile folder (C:\Users\<username>\).

Key hive files (per CertMaster):
• SAM — Security Accounts Manager; stores username information for accounts used on the current computer
• SECURITY — linked to the security database of the domain the current user is logged into
• SOFTWARE — settings for software and the Windows OS
• SYSTEM — settings for drivers and file systems
• DEFAULT — settings for the LocalSystem account profile
• NTUSER.DAT — per-user settings/preferences (in C:\Users\<username>\)
• USRCLASS.DAT — additional info per user class (in C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\)

⚠️ Note on CertMaster: the PDF text mislabels the SAM hive as "SYSTEM" in its first bullet (then lists "SYSTEM" a second time correctly). The SAM hive stores account credentials — this card uses the correct hive name.

front: 💻 What is the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), and what problem does it solve?
back:
The FHS is a collaborative document that specifies guidelines for the names and locations of files and directories on Linux systems.

Problem it solves: with many Linux distributions, having each place files wherever they wanted would break compatibility and make administration chaos. FHS lets software installers expect resources in specific locations and sysadmins anticipate where to find particular settings.

Most distributions are FHS-compliant, supporting compatibility with other systems.

💡 Display the FHS with the command ls /. The top-most directory is the root directory (/) — not the same as /root, which is the root user's home directory.

front: 💻 Give the Linux FHS standard subdirectories and their purpose.
back:
• /bin — essential command-line utilities/binaries (e.g., /bin/ls)
• /boot — files necessary to boot Linux
• /dev — hardware and software device drivers (e.g., /dev/sda1)
• /etc — basic configuration files (e.g., /etc/samba/smb.conf)
• /home — users' home directories
• /lib — shared program libraries
• /media — mount points for removable media (DVD-ROMs, USB)
• /mnt — mount points for temporarily mounting file systems from remote servers
• /opt — optional/large software packages (e.g., /opt/nessus for Nessus)
• /proc — virtual file system (VFS) representing continually updated kernel info
• /root — the root user's home directory
• /sbin — binaries used to complete the boot process; root-user executables (e.g., /sbin/ifconfig)
• /sys — another VFS storing device information
• /tmp — temporary files (may be lost on shutdown)
• /usr — read-only user programs and files (has subdirs /usr/bin, /usr/local, /usr/lib, /usr/lib64, /usr/share)
• /var — variable files that constantly change (log files, printer spools, some network configs)

💡 Four critical directories to memorize (per CertMaster): /etc, /home, /root, /var/log.

front: 💻 CertMaster names four critical Linux directories analysts should know. Name each and its role.
back:
• /etc — Configuration files for the system and its services. Firewall rules, SSH config, and software-management settings live here.

• /home — Each user's personal files. Users are placed here on login. Default: every user (except root) gets a subdirectory matching their username.

• /root — The root user's home directory. Do NOT confuse with the filesystem root /.

• /var/log — Where Linux and installed services write log files. First place a sysadmin or analyst looks when investigating a system issue.

💡 Shortcuts for the home directory:
• Variable: $HOME
• Tilde character: ~ (works in Korn, C shell, Bash)

⚠️ Exam trap: / is the filesystem root; /root is the root user's home. Two very different directories with confusingly similar names.

front: 💻 Where should you look on a Linux system for log files, and what does CertMaster say analysts do with them?
back:
✅ /var/log.

Linux and installed services typically write to log files stored there. As a sysadmin investigating a system issue or auditing system access, you'll likely find the information in log files in this directory.

💡 Common files inside /var/log/:
• auth.log or secure — authentication events
• syslog or messages — general system messages
• kern.log — kernel messages
• audit/audit.log — auditd records
• apache2/ or httpd/ — web server logs

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Logs are typically shipped from /var/log to a SIEM via rsyslog, syslog-ng, or Filebeat. Attackers often clear or truncate these logs — a sudden absence of log lines is itself an IoC.

front: 💻 What are system processes, and why do analysts need to be familiar with them?
back:
System processes are background tasks that run on a computer without user interaction — often without the user's knowledge. Examples: the OS kernel, system services, antivirus scans, disk defragmentation, user authentication, printing, updates.

Analysts need familiarity because:
1. Attackers will often attempt to hide their malicious programs as legitimate processes — masquerading with names close to real ones
2. Some system processes have had critical vulnerabilities — e.g., older versions of lsass.exe exploited to dump credentials or escalate privileges; the Shellshock vulnerability in Bash affected every Linux system
3. Recognizing "what should be running" is what makes "this shouldn't be running" obvious

💡 Baseline knowledge of legitimate processes is the difference between spotting lsass.exe running from an unusual path and just accepting "well, there's an lsass.exe."

front:
💻 Identify each of the following Windows system processes:

wininit.exe  lsass.exe  svchost.exe  explorer.exe  csrss.exe
back:
• wininit.exe — during boot, initializes critical Windows subsystems
• lsass.exe — Local Security Authority Subsystem Service; handles security policy, user authentication, and Active Directory management
• svchost.exe — generic host for running services; usually multiple instances, each hosting different Windows services
• explorer.exe — provides the graphical interface (taskbar, desktop)
• csrss.exe — Client/Server Runtime Subsystem; handles graphical instruction processing; essential for system stability

⚠️ Analyst hot spots:
• lsass.exe — target of credential-dumping tools like Mimikatz. Any process reading lsass.exe's memory that isn't antivirus is a huge red flag.
• svchost.exe — because multiple instances are normal, attackers name malware svhost.exe, scvhost.exe, or svchost.exe running from a non-System32 path. Always check the parent process and path.

front: 💻 Which Windows tool is used to view and manage running processes, and what should an analyst look for?
back:
✅ Task Manager.

From Task Manager, you can see which processes are running and the resources (CPU, memory, network, disk usage) they consume. You can sort by resource usage to identify potentially malicious processes using heavy resources.

What to look for:
• Processes you don't recognize (research and verify)
• Processes consuming unusual amounts of resources
• Processes running from unusual paths (a critical Windows process outside C:\Windows\System32)
• Multiple copies of a normally-single process

💡 More advanced tools: Process Explorer and Process Hacker (Sysinternals family) show parent-child relationships and open handles — much richer than Task Manager.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: In a real IR, "sort by CPU" is often the first triage move on a suspected host — cryptominers and unpacking malware light up CPU charts.

front:
💻 Which commands are used to view and manage Linux processes, and identify the following common processes:

init/systemd  sshd  cron  kthreadd  udevd
back:
Commands: ps, top, systemctl.

• init or systemd — the first process that starts, bootstrapping the OS and launching other services. Modern distros use systemd.
• sshd — handles incoming SSH connections for secure remote access
• cron — runs scheduled tasks and maintenance jobs
• kthreadd — handles kernel threads necessary for system operations
• udevd (systemd-udevd) — manages device events and hardware detection

💡 init/systemd is always PID 1 — the ancestor of every other process. On a compromised system, unexpected direct children of PID 1 are suspicious.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: cron is a top persistence-mechanism target on Linux. Attackers add malicious lines to /etc/crontab or user crontabs. Check for entries you don't recognize.

front: 🛡️ Why does CertMaster cite the 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack as a patch-management case study?
back:
WannaCry exploited a known Windows vulnerability (MS17-010, "EternalBlue") for which Microsoft had previously released a patch. Because many systems were not properly patched, WannaCry successfully infected hundreds of thousands of computers worldwide.

💡 The lesson isn't "zero-days are the problem" — the lesson is that failure to apply known patches is what enables large-scale ransomware campaigns. Effective patch management is one of the highest-return security investments an organization can make.

🔗 Historical context: EternalBlue was allegedly developed by the NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers group in April 2017. Microsoft patched it in March 2017 (before the leak). WannaCry launched in May 2017 — two months after the patch was available.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: WannaCry is one of the most-cited real-world incidents on the exam. Also cited for supply-chain awareness, ransomware response, and business-impact analysis.

front: 🛡️ CertMaster lists eight elements of a strong patch management strategy. Name them.
back:
1. An individual or task-specific team responsible for reviewing vendor newsletters and patch bulletins
2. Mechanisms to patch operating systems AND all applications running on them
3. Patch management principles that incorporate cloud resources
4. Assigning updates into urgent, important, and noncritical categories
5. A patch test environment for urgent/important patches before production
6. Detailed logging for monitoring and troubleshooting patch deployment
7. A method to evaluate firmware updates prior to deployment
8. Immediate push delivery for critical security patches
9. A routine schedule for noncritical patches

💡 Categorization is key: mission-critical systems get treated differently than desktops. Desktops are often patched as quickly as possible after a brief testing phase.

⚠️ Exam-relevant nuance: patch management can be manual, automated, or a combination. Automation is essential but usually requires occasional manual work to handle deployment errors.

front: 🛡️ What is patch testing, and what does CertMaster identify as the ideal test setup?
back:
Patch testing determines whether a software patch creates problems with the organization's unique mix of hardware, software, and configuration settings.

Two-stage approach:
1. Test on a single isolated system to check for crashes or instability
2. Deploy to a non-production environment hosting like-for-like mission-critical applications — including enterprise applications and networking systems

Validation goals:
• Confirm the patch removes the target vulnerability
• Confirm the patch does not introduce new vulnerabilities

💡 CertMaster emphasizes: vulnerability scans should verify that patches only resolve vulnerabilities and do not introduce any new ones.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: A "patched" system that scanners still flag as vulnerable — either because the patch failed silently or because the CVE was mis-attributed — is a common finding. Post-patch scanning closes that loop.

front: 🛡️ What is Configuration Management, and what four components does CertMaster identify?
back:
Configuration management uses a structured approach to maintaining consistent and secure system configurations across the organization. A proper CM system ensures systems are safe and only use approved configurations.

Components:
1. Baseline Configuration — create and document a standard baseline (disabling unnecessary services, applying least privilege, enforcing password policies)
2. Monitoring and Auditing — continuously monitor for adherence to the baseline; automated tools alert on changes (e.g., new unauthorized user accounts)
3. Change Management — formal process for requests and approvals to change a system configuration; minimizes risk of unapproved changes
4. Rollback Plans — plan to quickly undo configuration changes or patches that cause issues

💡 Baseline first. Without a documented baseline, you cannot detect drift, cannot audit compliance, and cannot roll back to a known-good state.

front: 🛡️ What benefits does a centralized configuration management system provide over per-endpoint configuration?
back:
• Consistency — configuration is defined once, applied to many systems
• Enforcement — the central management server overwrites changes made to an individual endpoint's configuration, preventing drift
• Near real-time visibility into configuration changes across the fleet
• Continuous compliance monitoring — any change to an endpoint generates an immediate alert
• Automated push of settings from a management server to endpoints

💡 Real-world tools that implement this pattern: Group Policy (Windows AD), Ansible, Puppet, Chef, SaltStack, Microsoft Intune, JAMF (macOS), MDM platforms.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: The security value is enormous — an attacker who modifies /etc/pam.d/ or a Windows registry auth setting sees their change reverted at the next config-management run. Detection + reversion becomes automatic.

front: 🔑 Expand these Module 3 acronyms: ASM, IoC, ICMP, ARP, SNMP, FTP, SSH, HTTP, DNS, NSE, STIX, TAXII, MISP, ISAC, CTA, AIS, CISA.
back:
Attack surface / discovery:
• ASM — Attack Surface Management
• IoC — Indicator of Compromise
• ICMP — Internet Control Message Protocol
• ARP — Address Resolution Protocol
• SNMP — Simple Network Management Protocol
• FTP — File Transfer Protocol
• SSH — Secure Shell
• HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol
• DNS — Domain Name System
• NSE — Nmap Scripting Engine

Threat intel:
• STIX — Structured Threat Information eXpression
• TAXII — Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information
• MISP — Malware Information Sharing Platform
• ISAC — Information Sharing and Analysis Center
• CTA — Cyber Threat Alliance
• AIS — Automated Indicator Sharing
• CISA — Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency

front: 🔑 Expand these Module 3 hardening/OS acronyms: NTFS, ext4, APFS, ADS, DLL, SAM, HKLM, HKCU, HKCR, HKU, HKCC, FHS, VFS, MFA, TOTP.
back:
File systems:
• NTFS — New Technology File System (Windows)
• ext4 — Fourth Extended Filesystem (Linux)
• APFS — Apple File System (macOS)
• ADS — Alternate Data Streams (NTFS feature)
• DLL — Dynamic-Link Library

Windows registry:
• SAM — Security Accounts Manager
• HKLM — HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
• HKCU — HKEY_CURRENT_USER
• HKCR — HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT
• HKU — HKEY_USERS
• HKCC — HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG

Linux & auth:
• FHS — Filesystem Hierarchy Standard
• VFS — Virtual File System
• MFA — Multi-Factor Authentication
• TOTP — Time-based One-Time Password

front: 🌐 Distinguish Infrastructure from Architecture in a networked environment.
back:
• Infrastructure — the hardware and physical components that make up the network: routers, switches, computers, servers, cables, wireless access points, and all other devices that allow data to flow.

• Architecture — the blueprint for how the infrastructure is organized, connected, and managed: network topology, IP addressing scheme, network segmentation, protocols used, and traffic routing.

💡 Rule of thumb: Infrastructure = things; Architecture = the plan for those things. You can have identical infrastructure inventories with completely different architectures.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: You cannot protect what you don't understand. Familiarity with your infrastructure and architecture is what turns a stream of alerts into an understandable story about what's happening.

Network Infrastructure and System Architecture

front: 🔄 What is a CI/CD pipeline, and what are its three stages?
back:
Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CI/CD) is the "assembly line for software development" — the backbone of moving applications from development to production.

1. Continuous Integration (CI) — code changes from multiple developers are committed to a shared repository. Each build is compiled and tested; failures notify the dev team. Establishes a stable codebase, catches bugs early, reduces integration conflicts.

2. Continuous Delivery (CD) — once tests pass, code is automatically sent to a staging area (test environment that mimics real-world). More advanced tests and security scans run here before release.

3. Continuous Deployment (also abbreviated CD) — a continuation of Continuous Delivery. Deployment to the live (production) environment is automated once all tests pass. No manual approval needed.

⚠️ Exam trap: both Delivery and Deployment are abbreviated CD. Delivery = automated push to staging (still needs approval to go live); Deployment = automated push all the way to production.

front: 🔄 CertMaster lists five practices for securing a CI/CD pipeline. Name them.
back:
1. Secure the code repository — MFA, access controls, role-based permissions, branch controls (all changes reviewed before merging)

2. Protect the build environment — isolate build servers, no direct Internet access, update/patch pipeline software

3. Scan for vulnerabilities early and often — automated static and dynamic code analysis during integration/testing; scan third-party tools regularly

4. Secure the deployment process — roll out to a small group first (canary/blue-green) for easy rollback

5. Mitigate supply chain attacks — use only trusted sources, known-good versions, integrity checks, and Software Composition Analysis (SCA) to detect unapproved, typosquatted, or vulnerable third-party packages

💡 If SCA flags a suspicious package, the build should fail and not proceed further — a "fail-closed" default.

front: 🐛 What is Software Composition Analysis (SCA), and what does typosquatting mean in this context?
back:
SCA — a class of tools that inspect third-party dependencies in a codebase to detect unapproved, vulnerable, or typosquatted packages.

Typosquatting in package ecosystems is when an attacker publishes a malicious package with a name that's a slight misspelling of a popular one (e.g., reqests vs. requests, colourama vs. colorama). Developers typo the install command and get the malicious package.

💡 SCA is one of the primary defenses against supply-chain compromise (Module 1 threat). It generates an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — Module 14 elaborates.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Common SCA tools include Snyk, Dependabot, GitHub Advanced Security, Sonatype Nexus, Black Duck. Enterprise dev teams integrate at least one into every CI pipeline.

front: ☁️ What does CertMaster want you to remember about "the cloud" from a security standpoint?
back:
Working "in the cloud" simply means you are renting space on someone else's hardware.

This framing matters because:
• Physical security is now someone else's responsibility
• The hardware is shared with unknown tenants (multi-tenancy)
• The provider can see (and must be trusted with) your infrastructure's low-level operations
• Legal jurisdiction depends on where the provider's data centers physically sit

💡 This is the foundation of the shared responsibility model covered in Lesson 4B — because the hardware isn't yours, some security controls become the CSP's duty and some remain yours.

front: ☁️ CertMaster names four key features of cloud-native infrastructure. List them with a one-line description of each.
back:
1. Scalability — apps can quickly grow or shrink depending on demand
2. Reliability — systems automatically recover or switch to backups if one part fails, greatly reducing downtime
3. Flexibility — updates and new features can be deployed seamlessly without taking the entire app offline
4. Automation — setup and management (like deploying new servers) happen automatically, reducing manual work and human error

💡 SRFA — "Scalable Reliable Flexible Automated". These are the "why cloud" bullets executives repeat.

front: ☁️ CertMaster identifies three cloud deployment models. Distinguish them.
back:
• Public Cloud — services hosted on third-party CSP infrastructure and accessed over the Internet. Best for orgs without budget/resources/desire to build their own. Examples: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, IBM Cloud, Oracle Cloud.

• Private Cloud — designed, built, and managed by an in-house team using hardware from a third-party CSP. High control, higher up-front capital and ongoing maintenance.

• Hybrid Cloud — combination of public and private. Merges on-premises infrastructure with public-cloud flexibility. Sensitive data stays private; non-sensitive workloads use public. Supports easy movement between clouds and disaster recovery.

💡 CertMaster's framing of the hybrid benefit: "best of both worlds" — adaptable/economical public cloud alongside secure/customized private cloud.

⚠️ Community cloud is a fourth model that appears in Security+ but is not listed in this CertMaster module.

front: ☁️ CertMaster lists three cloud-native security strategies analysts should focus on. Name them.
back:
1. Controlling access with identity management tools
2. Monitoring resources for suspicious activity
3. Using encryption for data-in-transit and at-rest

💡 CertMaster's framing: moving to the cloud does not make systems less secure. Many providers offer built-in tools for rapid updates and patching — but the organization must still be vigilant and implement strong practices.

🔗 The distinction of which party (customer vs. CSP) is responsible for each control is the shared responsibility model — covered in Lesson 4B.

front: 💻 Define virtualization and the role of the hypervisor.
back:
Virtualization is the ability to run multiple operating systems simultaneously on one physical system.

The hypervisor is the software that enables this. It manages virtual machines (VMs) — also known as guest OSs — by emulating hardware resources (CPU, memory, storage, peripherals) so each guest OS behaves as if it has exclusive access to the system.

💡 To function properly, VMs require drivers for the emulated hardware. Hypervisors may have limits on the types of guest OSs they support.

⚠️ The exam expects the terminology: host is the physical machine; guest is the VM; hypervisor is the software layer between them.

front: 💻 Distinguish Type 1 (Bare Metal) and Type 2 (Host-based) hypervisors, and name examples of each.
back:
• Type 1 — Bare Metal: installed directly onto the hardware, bypassing a host OS. Hardware only needs to meet the requirements of the hypervisor and guest OSs.
  Examples: VMware ESXi Server, Microsoft Hyper-V, Citrix XENServer.
  Best for: servers, data centers, production workloads.

• Type 2 — Host-based: installed on top of an existing host OS. The system must have enough resources to run both the host OS and the guest OSs through the hypervisor.
  Examples: VMware Workstation, Oracle VirtualBox, Parallels Workstation.
  Best for: desktops, testing, developer laptops.

💡 Performance rule: Type 1 is faster and more efficient (no host OS overhead). Type 2 is more convenient (runs alongside your normal workstation OS).

⚠️ Exam trap: memorize which examples are Type 1 vs Type 2. ESXi/Hyper-V/XEN = Type 1. Workstation/VirtualBox/Parallels = Type 2.

front: 💻 CertMaster lists five VM security risks. Name each with a one-line description.
back:
1. Hypervisor Vulnerabilities — if an attacker exploits the hypervisor, they may control all VMs on that host. A VM escape attack is when malware breaks out from a VM and interacts directly with the hypervisor.

2. VM Sprawl — VMs are so easy to create that organizations lose track of what's running, and important updates/patches get missed.

3. Snapshot and Cloning Risks — snapshots and clones (used for backups/testing) that are not properly encrypted and stored let an attacker access sensitive data simply by copying them.

4. Weak Network Isolation — improperly segmented VMs allow an attacker who compromises one VM to pivot to other VMs.

5. Misconfigured Resource Sharing — improper permissions/access-control lets an attacker create or alter VMs for persistence or evasion.

⚠️ VM escape is the marquee virtualization attack. Real-world example: Venom (CVE-2015-3456) targeting the QEMU floppy controller. Compromising the hypervisor is often "game over" for tenant isolation.

front: 💻 What is a VM escape attack?
back:
A VM escape is when malware inside a VM breaks out and interacts directly with the hypervisor — bypassing the isolation between the guest OS and the host.

Why it matters: the hypervisor manages all VMs on the host. If an attacker compromises it, they may gain control over every VM sharing that hypervisor — devastating in a multi-tenant environment.

💡 Mitigations:
• Keep the hypervisor patched
• Restrict hypervisor administrative access
• Segment VMs at the network layer (defense-in-depth)
• Detect anomalous guest→host system calls

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Cloud CSPs invest enormously in preventing tenant-to-tenant escape. It's essentially the worst-case failure mode for any public cloud.

front: 📦 What is containerization, and how does it differ from a VM?
back:
Containerization encapsulates all necessary components for software (code, libraries, and configurations) into a portable unit called a container. This ensures consistent application behavior regardless of the underlying platform.

Container vs VM:
• VM — includes a full guest OS. Each VM has its own kernel. Heavyweight.
• Container — shares the host OS kernel. Only includes the app, libraries, and binaries. Lightweight.

💡 Two most common container technologies:
• Docker — the most popular container platform (containers are often called "Docker containers")
• Kubernetes (K8s) — an orchestration tool that automatically deploys, scales, and secures multiple containers

⚠️ "K8s" spelling: K + 8 characters between + s. You will see this abbreviation frequently.

front: 📦 CertMaster lists four container benefits. Name them.
back:
1. Efficient — require fewer resources than a VM; start almost instantly; use less memory and storage
2. Portable — all components (including dependencies) packaged into a single container that runs on many machines
3. Consistent experience — the container guarantees the app works the same way regardless of where it runs
4. Support for microservices — big apps can be broken into small, manageable pieces; each microservice lives in its own container, making it easy to update and scale parts individually

💡 CertMaster's online-store example: web server in one container, database in another, payment processor in a third. Upgrading the payment processor only touches that one container.

front: 📦 CertMaster lists five container security risks. Name them and describe each.
back:
1. Shared Kernel Risk — all containers on a host share the same OS kernel, so any kernel vulnerability affects every container on that host

2. Escape Attacks — malware inside a compromised container can break out and infect the host or other containers

3. Insecure Images — containers launch from images (templates with code and dependencies). If the image has outdated/vulnerable software, every container from it inherits those flaws

4. Secrets Management — sensitive info (API keys, credentials) should NOT be stored in containers; if leaked, the app and data are compromised

5. Container Sprawl — like VM sprawl but for containers; without processes, orgs lose track of what containers are deployed

⚠️ Kernel-shared architecture is the fundamental container security tradeoff — containers are lightweight because they share the kernel, which is also their biggest attack surface.

front: 📦 Name the key container security best practices CertMaster recommends.
back:
• Monitor kernel logs for exploitation attempts, unusual system calls, or privilege escalation
• Only use images from trusted sources (or built in-house)
• Apply security patches to base images and rebuild containers often
• Perform vulnerability scans on container images before deploying
• Enforce principle of least privilege — minimum permissions for users
• Control container communication with firewall rules and network policies
• Store secrets externally (secret vaults), not inside container images
• Monitor and log containers for unusual traffic and processes

💡 "Secrets in external stores, not inside container images" is a CompTIA favorite. Real-world tooling: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Kubernetes Secrets (encrypted).

front: 🔗 What is an API, and give the analogy CertMaster uses.
back:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that allows two different software applications to talk to each other.

CertMaster analogy: the API is a messenger. Your smartwatch software does not need to know how the backend database is built — it just follows the rules the API provides. APIs define which requests the client can make and what responses will come back.

💡 Security uses: firewalls, SIEM platforms, and cloud services all use APIs to communicate. Example: use an API to pull threat intel from a third party and automatically update firewall rules. Scripted API interactions save time and reduce errors versus manual work.

front: 🔗 Name the six components of an API per CertMaster, and give the four HTTP methods commonly used.
back:
1. Requests and Responses — the conversation between client (requester) and server (responder)
2. Endpoints — URLs/paths for specific info. Example: online store /cart, SIEM /alerts, /logs
3. Methods — actions taken at the endpoint. Common HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE (CertMaster also lists PATCH in the diagram)
4. Data Format — standardized format for requests/responses. Typically JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) or XML (Extensible Markup Language)
5. Authentication — API keys, username/password, or special tokens
6. Documentation — explains endpoints, required auth, data formats, and possible responses

💡 HTTP method purposes:
• GET — retrieve data
• POST — create new data
• PUT — update/replace existing data
• PATCH — partially update data
• DELETE — remove data

front: 🔗 CertMaster lists four key steps to protect APIs. Name them.
back:
1. Require and enforce authentication and authorization for every API request
2. Rate limiting — cap how many times someone can use the API within a period, preventing endpoint abuse and overload
3. Encrypt data in transit with protocols like HTTPS
4. Monitor and log all API activity to detect suspicious behavior

💡 APIs are attack surfaces: unauthenticated APIs let attackers pull data directly. Rate limiting also mitigates enumeration attacks (walking through user IDs) and credential stuffing.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: The OWASP API Security Top 10 is essential reading for anyone auditing API-heavy applications. It expands substantially on this CertMaster list.

front: 🔐 What is Zero Trust Network Architecture (ZTNA), and what is its guiding principle?
back:
ZTNA is a modern security-focused network architecture built around the concept "Never Trust. Always Verify."

It replaces the traditional model of implicit trust for anything "inside" the perimeter. ZTNA assumes that any part of the network can be compromised at any time.

To address that assumption, ZTNA embraces deperimeterization: it eliminates reliance on traditional network-boundary security measures and focuses on continuous authorization, no matter where the request is coming from.

💡 Why the shift: traditional "hard shell, soft center" networks worked when everything was on-premises. Cell phones, remote work, and cloud make the perimeter obsolete — attackers can access resources from anywhere.

⚠️ Exam mnemonic: "Never Trust, Always Verify" is the phrase associated with ZTNA. Any answer choice with this phrase is almost always ZTNA-related.

front: 🔐 What is Continuous Authorization in ZTNA, and how does it differ from traditional authentication?
back:
Continuous Authorization challenges every access attempt and requires repeated verification and strict permission checks — instead of granting implicit trust after one-time login.

• Traditional — one-time verification during initial access. Once granted, the user roams freely.

• Continuous Authorization — ongoing assessment; even after access is granted, the user's actions are continuously scrutinized to ensure they adhere to policy and don't exhibit anomalous behavior.

Common verification methods: MFA, device compliance checks, context-aware policies.

💡 Rule of thumb: continuous authorization is always evaluating. If the user's risk score jumps mid-session (unusual geo, sudden bulk downloads), continuous authorization can revoke access without waiting for the next login.

front: 🔐 What is an Identity Provider (IdP) in ZTNA?
back:
The IdP stores and manages identity information for users, devices, and applications. It's a core ZTNA component — the "gatekeeper" for network resources.

IdP functions:
• Manages authentication
• Enforces security policies (e.g., verifying MFA is enabled, verifying login location)
• Enables SSO — Single Sign-On: user authenticates once, gets a security token, uses it to access multiple applications without re-logging
• Continues to verify each new request meets the appropriate requirements

💡 Real-world IdPs: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), Okta, Ping Identity, Google Workspace, Auth0.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: IdP logs are gold. Sign-in logs from Entra or Okta show every authentication attempt with geo, device, and risk-score context — invaluable for identity-attack investigation.

front: 🔐 Distinguish Continuous Authorization from Context-Based Re-authentication. Both are ZTNA concepts.
back:
• Continuous Authorization — constantly monitoring and evaluating trust in real time throughout the entire session. Dynamically adjusts permissions based on ongoing analysis of behavior, context, and risk. Proactive, always-on.

• Context-Based Re-authentication — re-verifies identity and device context at specific points during an active session, or when specific risk factors are detected (unusual location, unfamiliar device, sensitive resource access). Trigger-based safeguard.

💡 Analogy: continuous authorization is a security guard walking the floor watching everyone. Context-based re-authentication is a locked door that pops up when a user tries to enter a sensitive area.

Technologies supporting context-based re-auth (per CertMaster):
• MFA
• Behavioral Analytics
• Device Posture Checks
• Risk-Based Authentication

Real-world products: Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access, Okta Adaptive MFA.

front: 🌐 What is network segmentation, and what standards recommend it?
back:
Network segmentation is the technique of splitting a network and its nodes into several portions. A prominent segmentation technique is subnetting — the logical division of a network into multiple subnetworks.

Standards and regulations that recommend or require network segmentation:
• NIST standards
• FISMA (Federal Information Security Management Act)
• PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)

💡 Basic principle: protect sensitive data by ensuring that an individual segment's failure does not impact the larger enterprise network. A compromise in the guest Wi-Fi should never reach the PCI cardholder data environment.

front: 🌐 What are VLANs, and how does CertMaster's example use them?
back:
Virtual LANs (VLANs) logically segment endpoints in one network from endpoints in another. They are defined via software running on switches, allowing a single physical device to separate network traffic as if multiple physical switches were used.

💡 CertMaster example: put databases containing sensitive enterprise transactions in one VLAN and public-facing web servers in a different VLAN. If an attacker launches a DoS against the web servers, it's easier to restrict the attack and protect the availability of the databases in the other VLAN.

⚠️ Key concept: VLANs are logical, not physical. They use tagged frames (IEEE 802.1Q) to route traffic across shared physical infrastructure while keeping it segregated.

front: 🌐 What is microsegmentation, and how does it differ from traditional segmentation? Include the north-south vs east-west traffic distinction.
back:
Microsegmentation isolates workloads from one another and protects them individually.

• Traditional segmentation focuses on client-to-server interactions ("north-south" traffic — traffic in and out of the data center)

• Modern cloud environments have more traffic between systems and applications within the same network ("east-west" traffic)

• Microsegmentation uses Software-Defined Networks (SDN) to establish policies that limit traffic between workloads — controlling east-west flow that traditional perimeter segmentation ignores.

💡 Rule of thumb: north-south = perimeter traffic; east-west = internal traffic. Microsegmentation is essential in cloud/microservices because most traffic never touches the perimeter.

⚠️ Exam trap: north-south and east-west are directional metaphors from network diagrams, not literal compass directions. If a stem describes "container-to-container communication," think east-west.

front: 🌐 Name the three planes of a Software-Defined Network (SDN) and describe what each does.
back:
• Control Plane — makes decisions about how traffic should be prioritized and secured, and where it should be switched

• Data Plane — handles the actual switching and routing of traffic and enforces Access Control Lists (ACLs) for security

• Management Plane — monitors traffic conditions and network status

💡 Simple mental model: Control = brain, Data = muscles, Management = eyes.

💡 The SDN controller application interfaces with network devices using APIs. It defines policy on the control plane; devices implement it on the data plane.

front: 🌐 What's the difference between an SDN Northbound API and a Southbound API?
back:
• Northbound API — interface between the SDN applications and the SDN controller. Applications tell the controller what policies to enforce.

• Southbound API — interface between the controller and the network appliances. The controller tells the devices how to forward traffic and apply rules.

💡 Directional mnemonic: applications sit "above" (north of) the controller in typical SDN diagrams; network devices sit "below" (south of) it. Northbound = up to apps; Southbound = down to hardware.

⚠️ Exam trap: OpenFlow is a well-known southbound protocol. REST APIs are common on northbound interfaces.

front: 🔐 CertMaster names three elements that ensure the security and integrity of a Zero Trust architecture. List and describe each.
back:
1. Asset Identification — continuously and accurately recognizing every device that accesses the network. Uses EDR, NAC, and device-management tools. Tracks by a unique identifier (MAC address or digital certificate).

2. Asset Management — strict controls over device configuration, software update installation, and compliance. Enforced via configuration management systems, centralized patch management, endpoint protection, and SDN.

3. Asset Attestation — verifies devices continuously meet required security measures before granting access. Ongoing device "health checks" validate endpoint protection status, encryption, patch level, firewall status, etc.

💡 Note the acronyms surfaced:
• EDR — Endpoint Detection and Response
• NAC — Network Access Control
• IoT — Internet of Things (device category to be tracked)

front: 🔐 Distinguish agent-based and agentless ZTNA implementations, and note the tradeoff.
back:
• Agent-based — a small software client (agent) is installed on each device. The agent monitors and gathers info and sends it back to the ZTNA controller. Security policies are monitored and enforced at the device level.

• Agentless — no software installed on local systems. Users authenticate through a secure portal using standard web protocols. Works well with BYOD; quick to deploy.

💡 Tradeoff: agentless is faster to deploy and BYOD-friendly, but it does not provide the same level of enforcement for security posture as agent-based (no host-level telemetry, no ability to verify patch level or endpoint protection status directly).

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: In practice, most enterprises run hybrid — agents on managed devices, agentless portal access for contractors and BYOD.

front: 🔐 CertMaster identifies limitations of ZTNA. What are they, and what does the "not set-it-and-forget-it" framing mean?
back:
ZTNA reduces many threats and attack surfaces but does not eliminate all of them.

Threats ZTNA cannot fully stop:
• Credential/authentication attacks (phishing, social engineering)
• Personal devices not meeting security baselines
• Insider threats

Implementation weaknesses:
• Failing to enforce least privilege
• Overlooking IT assets (missing them from inventory)
• Insufficient monitoring
• Users bypassing security due to frustration

💡 CertMaster explicit: ZTNA is not a "set it and forget it" implementation. Policies and procedures must be constantly monitored and updated. Endpoint controls, user education, and continuous monitoring are still required alongside ZTNA.

front: ☁️ What is SASE, and what services does it converge?
back:
SASE — Secure Access Service Edge — is a networking architecture that merges networking and cybersecurity into a single cloud-delivered service. Everything used to connect and protect users (firewalls, Zero Trust controls, secure web gateways, routers, VPNs) works together regardless of where users and devices are located.

SASE is a confluence of:
• WAN — Wide Area Network services
• CASB — Cloud Access Security Broker
• FWaaS — Firewall as a Service
• Zero Trust

💡 Why SASE emerged: traditionally, security appliances were installed in the data center. With remote work and cloud apps, this created bottlenecks and gaps. SASE brings the network and security to the cloud, so policies follow the user regardless of location.

⚠️ Pronounced "sassy." Coined by Gartner in 2019.

front: ☁️ SASE benefits for the cybersecurity analyst — CertMaster names three. What are they?
back:
1. Centralized Visibility — user activity, anomalies, and incidents are easier to manage because all security and networking controls are unified and managed from the cloud
2. Consistent Policies — security policies are applied the same way to all users and devices regardless of physical location
3. Faster Response — better visibility + automated tools = detect and respond to threats faster, decreasing risks and downtime

💡 CertMaster's example scenario: a phishing attack targeting remote users. In a traditional network, remote users are outside the physical perimeter and harder to protect. With SASE, all users have their internet traffic inspected, threats blocked, and activity logged regardless of location — the analyst can quickly respond.

⚠️ CertMaster also names three SASE features by category: IAM, secure web gateways, Zero Trust network access. Real-world SASE product examples cited: Cisco Umbrella, Cisco Web Security Appliance, F5 BIG-IP, Palo Alto Networks, AWS WAF, Cisco AMP.

front: ☁️ What is cloud bursting, and what problem does it solve?
back:
Cloud bursting: when workload runs on the private cloud under typical load, and excess traffic/workload bursts into the public cloud when demand spikes.

Problem solved: right-sizes on-premises capacity. Instead of provisioning private-cloud capacity for peak demand (expensive, mostly idle), you run at baseline privately and rent public-cloud capacity during peaks.

💡 Requires:
• Applications architected to run in both environments
• Secure, high-bandwidth connection between clouds
• Consistent identity/policy so bursted workloads are still governed

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Bursted workloads can be a blind spot — logs, network monitoring, and IdP integration must span both environments or the burst-into-public phase runs without SOC visibility.

front: ☁️ What is data partitioning in a hybrid cloud, and why is it used?
back:
Data partitioning: sensitive/regulated data is stored on the private cloud, while web servers and less-sensitive data are hosted in the public cloud.
