🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: In practice, analysts pick the language that fits the target — Bash for Linux hosts, PowerShell for Windows/Active Directory work, Python for anything that needs libraries or cross-platform portability. Expect exam scenarios that hinge on picking the right language for the target OS.

front: 📝 What are the four elements of a well-written script per CertMaster?
back:
1. Parameters — input data passed to the script as arguments
2. Branching and looping statements — alter flow of execution based on conditions
3. Validation and error handlers — check inputs and ensure robust execution
4. Unit tests — ensure the script returns expected outputs given expected inputs

⚠️ A script missing input validation is a common source of both bugs AND security vulnerabilities (command injection, path traversal in the script itself).

front: 📝 What is syntax in the context of a scripting language?
back:
The syntax of a language is the set of rules that constrains:
• how sections of code are laid out in blocks
• the standard statements available (branching, looping constructs, etc.)

Every scripting language has its own syntax — Bash, PowerShell, and Python each use different characters to end an if block, different ways to define variables, and different loop keywords.

⚠️ CertMaster repeats this warning three times in Module 11 — the exam will test whether you can match syntax fragments (fi, }, indentation) to the right language.

front: 🛡️ How do scripts relate to SOAR and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
back:
• SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) systems use scripts to automate gathering logs, generating security alerts, and performing enrichment/response steps.

• Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is built on scripts and code — instead of manually configuring network systems, IaC lets you manage them through repeatable, version-controlled scripts.

💡 Scripts are the substrate under both — SOAR playbooks are essentially chained scripts triggered by security events; IaC (Terraform, Ansible, CloudFormation) is scripts describing desired infrastructure state.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: SOAR and IaC both appear elsewhere in the objectives (1.5 and 1.6). Module 11 establishes scripts as the foundation those higher-level frameworks depend on.

front: 📝 What is a variable in a script, and what problem does it solve?
back:
A variable is a named storage location in your script that holds a value (a text string, number, etc.) which can be referenced by name throughout the script.

Problem it solves: instead of hard-coding the same value in many places, you assign it to a variable once and reference the variable — making the code flexible and easy to update.

💡 The variable's value can stay the same or change throughout the script — that is optional, not required.

front: 📝 Distinguish local variables from environment variables.
back:
• Local variables — defined and used only in that specific script or program. They do not persist outside the script and other scripts cannot see them.

• Environment variables — defined by the OS or user and applies to the system as a whole. Can be used by all scripts and programs running in that environment.

💡 Examples of environment variables you'll see on the exam / in the field:
• Linux: $PATH, $HOME, $USER
• Windows: %USERPROFILE%, %APPDATA%, %PATH%

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Attackers frequently abuse environment variables — planting malicious binaries in a directory that appears early in $PATH, or storing tokens in %APPDATA% subdirectories.

front: 📝 What is variable substitution (a.k.a. parameter expansion)?
back:
The act of referencing or retrieving the value of a variable — so the interpreter substitutes the variable's current value in place of the variable name.

💡 Each language has its own retrieval syntax:
• Bash: $var or ${var}
• PowerShell: $var
• Python: use the variable name directly, or f"..." f-strings for interpolation

Substitution is what makes scripts flexible — you write logic once, and the same code produces different results based on the current variable values.

front:
📝 Interpret this PowerShell snippet. What does it output?

$myVariable = 10
Write-Output "The value is $myVariable"
back:
Output: The value is 10

Explanation:
• $myVariable = 10 — assigns the value 10 to the variable $myVariable (PowerShell uses $ in the variable name itself, not just for retrieval).
• Write-Output "The value is $myVariable" — writes the string to output. Because it's in double quotes, PowerShell expands $myVariable to its value.

⚠️ In PowerShell, as in Bash, double quotes allow variable expansion but single quotes do not. Change the quotes to single and it would print the literal string The value is $myVariable.

front: 📝 What is an array, and why use one instead of many individual variables?
back:
An array is a collection of values stored in a single variable — an ordered sequence accessed by index.

Benefits over separate variables:
• Simpler code when performing the same operation on many values
• Easier maintenance — update the array once and every reference sees the change
• Lets you iterate over the collection with a loop instead of writing repetitive code

💡 Arrays are the natural data structure for a for loop to iterate over.

front: 📝 How are array elements indexed, and what index does the first element occupy?
back:
Arrays are organized as an ordered sequence based on their index. The index starts at 0 and increases from there.

• First element → index 0
• Second element → index 1
• Third element → index 2
• and so on

💡 This zero-based indexing is the "fundamental component" of arrays — it's what lets you access, modify, and remove values by referencing their place in the array rather than each individual variable name.

⚠️ Common bug pattern: off-by-one errors when analysts assume the first element is at index 1.

front:
📝 What does this Bash line do?

my_arr=(1 "Hello" 3.1)
back:
Performs a compound assignment to a Bash array named my_arr — assigns all three values at once.

Result — the indexes are set by the order the values are listed:
• my_arr[0] = 1
• my_arr[1] = "Hello"
• my_arr[2] = 3.1

Bash compound assignment syntax uses parentheses with values separated by spaces (not commas).

front:
📝 What is the difference between these two Bash lines?

A) my_arr=(1 "Hello" 3.1)
B) my_arr[0]=1 my_arr[1]="Hello" my_arr[2]=3.1
back:
Both end with an identical array, but they use different assignment styles:

A) Compound assignment — parentheses set the whole array at once; values are auto-indexed by their position (first value → index 0, second → index 1, etc.).

B) Individual assignment — each value is placed at a specific index using square brackets. Most languages allow this style too, useful when you need to update a single element or fill an array sparsely.

front:
📝 In Bash, what will the following print, and what is the syntax rule for referencing an array?

my_arr=(1 "Hello" 3.1)
echo ${my_arr[0]}
back:
Output: 1

Bash array reference syntax rules:
• Wrap the array reference in curly braces: ${my_arr[...]}
• The index goes inside square brackets
• Prefix with $ to retrieve the value

⚠️ Without the curly braces, Bash misparses $my_arr[0] — it evaluates $my_arr (giving you only the first element) followed by the literal characters [0].

front:
📝 What is the difference between these Bash references, and what does each return?

A) ${my_arr[0]}
B) ${my_arr[*]}
back:
A) Specific index — returns only the element at index 0 (the first element).

B) All values — the asterisk (*) as the index returns every value in the array. The at symbol (@) works the same way: ${my_arr[@]}.

💡 * and @ are near-equivalent in this context, but there is a subtle difference in how they behave inside quoted strings — "${arr[*]}" produces a single word; "${arr[@]}" produces one word per element (useful when passing arrays to functions).

front: 📝 What is a string literal, and when is it used?
back:
A string literal is any fixed value that represents a string of text within the source code.

Used when you want items like numbers, letters, symbols, and even spaces to be treated like text — not evaluated as commands or variables.

Typical uses:
• Defining file paths
• Outputting sentences and text to the screen
• Processing data as text

💡 String literals are usually enclosed in quotation marks — either single (' ') or double (" ") depending on the language.

front: 📝 In Bash, what is the difference between single-quoted and double-quoted string literals?
back:
• Single quotes (' ') — string is treated literally. Variables and special characters inside are NOT expanded.

• Double quotes (" ") — allows variable expansion. $name is replaced with its value.

Example:
my_string='Hello, world!'  # literal
name="Alice"
greeting="Hello, $name!"  # expands to "Hello, Alice!"

⚠️ If the greeting line used single quotes, it would print literally as Hello, $name! — the $name would NOT expand.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Attackers exploit this distinction constantly — command injection payloads use double quotes or backticks to trigger substitution, then close them at inconvenient moments.

front: 📝 What are metacharacters in a scripting language?
back:
Metacharacters are special characters that have reserved meanings in a language. They can cause problems if you need to use them as a literal character rather than for their special function.

Typical metacharacters called out in CertMaster:
• New-line, space, and tab keystrokes
• Asterisk (*)   • Question mark (?)
• Square brackets ([ ])
• Single quote (')   • Double quote (")
• Backslash (\)   • Dollar sign ($)
• Semicolon (;)   • Ampersand (&)
• Parentheses (( ))   • Pipe (|)
• Caret (^)   • Angle brackets (< >)

front: 📝 What is an escape character, and how does it differ from a string literal?
back:
An escape character is used to remove the special meaning from a metacharacter so it can be treated literally.

Difference from a string literal:
• A string literal (quotes) removes special meaning from an entire span of characters at once.
• An escape character removes the special meaning from one character at a time.

💡 Example — Bash uses backslash (\) as its escape character. To display $1,000, you write "\$1,000". Without the backslash, Bash would try to interpret $1 as a positional parameter.

front: 📝 In Bash, what is the escape character, and what does "\$1,000" print?
back:
The Bash escape character is the backslash (\).

The string "\$1,000" prints as: $1,000

Why: the $ normally identifies a variable — Bash would try to expand $1 as the first positional parameter. The backslash tells Bash to treat the very next character ($) as a literal, so the string outputs as a monetary amount.

front: 📝 What is a function in scripting, and what does calling one accomplish?
back:
A function is a block of code that can be reused to perform a specific task.

Benefits of calling a function:
• Efficiency — you do not need to repeatedly write the same or similar code
• Functions can be defined once and called from anywhere in the script (or even from other scripts)
• Functions can accept arguments/parameters to customize behavior for different data
• The output can be reused later in the script or produce an effect (like printing to screen)

💡 Like variables, functions have a unique identifier — that's the name you use to call them.

front:
📝 What does this Python function do, and what does def mean?

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Carl")
back:
Defines a function named greet that takes one parameter (name) and prints a personalized greeting. Calling greet("Carl") prints: Hello, Carl!

Syntax breakdown:
• def — Python keyword that defines a function
• greet — function's unique identifier
• (name) — parameter list
• The indented block below def is the function's body (Python uses indentation to define blocks — no braces or end keyword)
• f"Hello, {name}!" — an f-string that inserts the value of name directly into the string

front: 📝 What is a comment in a script, and how is it typically marked?
back:
A comment is a way to annotate code so it is easier for the author and other programmers to understand what the code is doing. Comments are ignored by the interpreter or compiler.

Comment marker in the majority of languages:
• # — everything after the pound/number sign on that line is a comment
• Used by: Bash, Python, PowerShell (also supports <# ... #> for block comments)

💡 Good practice:
• Include comment(s) at the top explaining what the script does
• Comment each line or code block that requires explanation
• Avoid commenting on lines with obvious purpose — too many comments clutter the source and make it harder to understand

front: 📝 What is an exit code (a.k.a. exit status), and what does exit code 0 mean?
back:
An exit code is the value returned at the end of a script that tells the system whether the script ran successfully.

Convention:
• Exit code 0 = SUCCESS (the script executed successfully)
• Any other value = FAILURE (something went wrong)

💡 Why exit codes matter:
• They let the script communicate results to whatever called it
• They enable multi-step scripts to respond intelligently to failures — you can chain steps so the next only runs if the previous exited with 0

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: In shell scripts, exit codes are typically checked with $? (the previous command's exit code). Non-zero codes trigger error-handling branches or halt the pipeline.

front:
📝 What does this Bash script do, and what does the shebang line accomplish?

#!/bin/bash
filename="test.txt"
if [ -f "$filename" ]; then
    echo "The file '$filename' exists."
    exit 0
else
    echo "The file '$filename' does not exist."
    exit 1
fi
back:
Checks whether a file called test.txt exists in the current directory. If it does, prints a success message and exits with 0 (success). If not, prints a failure message and exits with 1 (failure).

Line-by-line:
• #!/bin/bash — the shebang line; tells the OS which interpreter to use to run this script
• filename="test.txt" — variable assignment
• if [ -f "$filename" ] — the -f test returns true if the file exists AND is a regular file
• exit 0 / exit 1 — sets the exit status returned to whatever ran the script
• fi — end of the if block in Bash

front: 📝 What is redirection in scripting, and what does it enable?
back:
Redirection allows the output of commands to be sent to other locations (such as a file or another program) and allows the input for a script to come from somewhere other than the keyboard (like a file or another script's output).

Handled by redirectors — specific special characters:
• > — redirect output to a file (overwrite)
• < — take input from a file
• >> — append output to a file (do not overwrite)
• | — pipe output of one command as input to another

💡 Without redirection, script output would only be visible on the screen — no way to log results, chain commands, or feed pre-recorded input.

front:
📝 What does each of these redirectors do?

A) >
B) <
C) >>
D) |
back:
A) Greater-than (>) — redirects output to a file (overwrites). Example: Get-ChildItem > filelist.txt

B) Less-than (<) — takes input from a file.

C) Double greater-than (>>) — appends output to the specified file (preserves existing content).

D) Pipe (|) — sends the output of one command as the input of another.

⚠️ Common exam trap: > vs >>. Single-arrow overwrites and destroys existing file contents; double-arrow appends. Getting this wrong in a real log-collection script can silently wipe your logs.

front:
📝 What does this command do, and what would the output be if the directory contains files named salt1.txt, salt2.doc, data.csv, mysaltfile.pdf, and notes.txt?

ls | grep "salt"
back:
Runs ls to list the directory contents, then pipes that output as input to grep "salt", which filters for lines containing the string "salt".

Output:
salt1.txt
salt2.doc
mysaltfile.pdf

The pipe (|) is the operator making this work — ls alone lists everything; grep "salt" alone would wait for input from the keyboard. Chaining them with a pipe filters ls's output on-the-fly.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: | is the workhorse of Linux log analysis — think cat auth.log | grep "Failed password" | wc -l to count failed SSH auth attempts.

front: 📝 What does the PowerShell command Get-ChildItem > filelist.txt do?
back:
Runs Get-ChildItem (PowerShell's equivalent of Linux ls — lists files and directories in the current location) and redirects the output to a file named filelist.txt, overwriting any existing content in that file.

💡 If filelist.txt already contained data, it will be replaced. To append instead, use >>.

front: 📝 What is a loop in scripting?
back:
A loop is any control statement that executes code repeatedly based on a certain condition.

Loops let you keep a block of code active until it is no longer needed — indispensable for processing lists, monitoring conditions, or repeating an action a specific number of times.

💡 CertMaster names three types: while, until, and for. The two universal types across languages are while and for.

front: 📝 Distinguish the three loop types: while, until, and for.
back:
• while loop — runs the code block while a condition is true. Exits when the condition becomes false.

• until loop — runs the code block until a condition becomes true. In other words: runs while the condition is false, then exits.

• for loop — executes the code block for a specified number of times (or once per element in an iterable). Does not depend on a condition being true/false to start or stop.

💡 while and until are inverses of each other. for is the natural loop for iterating over arrays and known ranges.

front:
📝 What does this Bash while loop do, and what is the purpose of ((var++))?

var=1
while [ $var -le 5 ]; do
    echo "The current number is $var."
    ((var++))
done
back:
Prints "The current number is 1." through "The current number is 5.", then exits.

How it works:
• Condition tested: is $var less-than-or-equal-to 5? (-le is Bash's letter-based comparison operator)
• As long as the condition is true, the code under do runs
• ((var++)) is the iterator — adds 1 to $var each pass through the loop

⚠️ Without the iterator, $var would stay at 1 forever, the condition would never become false, and you would have an infinite loop. Every real while loop needs some way to progress toward the exit condition.

front: 📝 What is an iterator in a loop, and what happens if you forget one in a while loop?
back:
An iterator is code inside the loop that updates the value being tested by the loop's condition — typically by incrementing (or decrementing) a counter variable.

💡 Iterators are what make loops progress toward their exit condition. Without an iterator:
• The tested variable never changes
• The condition never becomes false
• The loop never exits — this is an infinite loop

Examples:
• Bash: ((var++))
• Python: i += 1 (or use range() in a for loop that iterates automatically)
• PowerShell: $i++

front:
📝 What does this Python for loop output?

var = ["Kai", "Ali", "Joseph"]
for i in var:
    print(f"{i} is a member of the team.")
back:
Output:
Kai is a member of the team.
Ali is a member of the team.
Joseph is a member of the team.

How it works:
• var = ["Kai", "Ali", "Joseph"] creates a list — Python lists use square brackets with comma-separated items
• for i in var: iterates over each element in the list
• On each pass, the current element is assigned to the iterator variable i
• The loop runs exactly 3 times, once per list element

💡 A Python for loop iterates automatically over each item in the sequence — no manual iterator required. This makes for loops ideal for processing arrays/lists.

front:
📝 What does this PowerShell for loop output, and what do the three parts inside the parentheses control?

for ($i = 1; $i -le 5; $i++) {
    Write-Output "The current number is $i."
}
back:
Iterates exactly 5 times, printing "The current number is 1." through "The current number is 5."

The three parts inside the parentheses:
1. $i = 1 — initialization: set $i to 1 before the loop starts
2. $i -le 5 — condition: continue while $i is less-than-or-equal-to 5
3. $i++ — iterator: increment $i by 1 each pass

💡 This "C-style" three-part for loop is common in PowerShell, JavaScript, C/C++, and Java — but Python and Bash use different for syntax (Python iterates directly over a sequence; Bash uses for var in list; do ... done).

front: 📝 What is a control statement, and what does it enable?
back:
A control statement begins a section of code that defines the order in which instructions are executed.

By controlling the flow of instructions, control statements let a script follow one or more paths based on circumstances — instead of running every line every time.

💡 Categories of control statements you'll encounter:
• Conditional statements (if, if...else, elif, switch/case)
• Loop statements (while, for, until)
• Jump statements (break, continue, return)

front: 📝 What is a conditional statement?
back:
A conditional statement is a control statement that tells the program it must make a decision based on various factors.

How it works:
• If the program evaluates the factors as true, it continues to execute the code in the conditional
• If the evaluation is false, the program does not execute that code

💡 Conditional statements are fundamental to most programs because they let the script respond differently based on input, environment, or prior results.

front: 📝 How does each language mark the end of an if statement: Bash, PowerShell, and Python?
back:
• Bash — uses fi (the word "if" reversed)
• PowerShell — uses a closing curly brace }
• Python — does not use a special character; instead, the end is marked by removing the indentation

⚠️ High-value exam distinction. Seeing fi, esac, or done in a snippet immediately identifies the language as Bash. Seeing indentation-only structure signals Python.

💡 Bash uses the same reversed-word pattern elsewhere: case ... esac, but while ... done and for ... done break the pattern.

front:
📝 What does this Bash if statement do, and what is the role of each keyword?

var=5
if [ "$var" -gt 1 ]; then
    echo "$var is greater than 1!"
fi
back:
Outputs: 5 is greater than 1!

Keyword roles:
• if [ ... ] — the condition to be evaluated, wrapped in square brackets
• -gt — Bash's letter-based comparison operator for "greater than"
• then — begins the block of code that runs if the condition is true
• echo "..." — prints the message to the screen
• fi — ends the entire if statement

Since 5 > 1 evaluates true, the echo runs. If $var were 1 or less, nothing would happen.

front: 📝 What is the basic syntax of a Bash if statement?
back:
if [ <condition to be evaluated> ]; then
    <code to execute if condition is true>
fi

Structural rules:
• Condition goes inside square brackets, with a space after [ and before ]
• The line ends with ; then (or then on the next line)
• The block ends with fi

front: 📝 What does the else keyword add to an if statement, and what about elif?
back:
• if...else — enables a choice between two actions. If the condition is true, the first action runs; otherwise, the action following else runs.

• elif ("else if") — used when there are more than two possible branches. One or more elif clauses specify additional conditions to evaluate before falling through to else.

💡 Language equivalents of elif:
• Bash: elif
• Python: elif
• PowerShell: elseif (one word)

front: 📝 What is the basic syntax of a Bash if...else statement?
back:
if [ <condition to be evaluated> ]; then
    <code to execute if condition is true>
else
    <code to execute if condition is false>
fi

💡 The else block runs only when the if condition is false. Only one branch executes per pass.

front: 📝 What is the basic syntax of a Bash if...elif statement?
back:
if [ <condition to be evaluated> ]; then
    <code to execute if condition is true>
elif [ <other condition to be evaluated> ]; then
    <code to execute if other condition is true>
fi

💡 You can chain multiple elif clauses. Conditions are evaluated top-to-bottom and the first true block runs; subsequent branches are skipped.

front:
📝 What does this Bash snippet do, and what do $? and 2> /dev/null mean?

chmod 888 file 2> /dev/null
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Permissions set successfully."
    exit 0
else
    echo "Could not set permissions."
    exit 1
fi
back:
Attempts to run chmod 888 file. If it succeeds (exit code 0) prints the success message and exits 0. If not, prints an error message and exits 1.

Key mechanics:
• $? — special Bash variable that holds the exit code of the most recent command. -eq 0 tests whether it equals 0.
• 2> /dev/null — redirects stderr (file descriptor 2) to the null device, suppressing the default error message that chmod would print. This lets the custom echo handle the error output cleanly.

⚠️ In this example the chmod 888 command will fail because 888 is not a valid permissions setting — permission bits max out at 7 per octet (rwx).

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: This pattern — command, check $?, branch — is the backbone of automated remediation scripts and every SOAR-style shell playbook.

front: 📝 What is the difference between operators and operands?
back:
• Operators — objects that evaluate expressions in various ways (perform arithmetic, comparison, logical evaluation, string manipulation, etc.)
• Operands — the values being operated on by the operator

💡 Example: in the expression 1 == 2:
• == is the operator
• 1 and 2 are the operands
• The expression evaluates to false

front: 📝 What are the three main categories of operators, and what does each do?
back:
• Arithmetic (numerical) operators — perform mathematical operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and more advanced math.

• Boolean (logical) operators — connect multiple values so they can be evaluated together. Express rules such as AND, OR, NOT.

• String operators — manipulate strings in various ways: concatenating strings, returning a specific character (also called slicing), verifying whether a character exists in a string, etc.

💡 A fourth category — comparison operators (==, !=, -gt, -le) — is sometimes grouped under Boolean since it returns a true/false result.

front: 📝 What is the difference between == and =? Why does this distinction matter?
back:
• == (double equal) — comparison operator. Evaluates whether the operands have equal values. Returns true or false.

• = (single equal) — assignment operator. Assigns a value to a variable.

Example:
• 1 == 2 → outputs false
• x = 5 → assigns 5 to x

⚠️ Confusing these is a classic bug. Writing if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5) in a C-family language assigns 5 to x and always evaluates true — the intended comparison never happens. The exam will test whether you recognize this.

front: 📝 What is letter-based comparison syntax, and where do you see it?
back:
Some languages don't use the traditional symbolic comparison operators (>, <, >=, <=) — they use letter-based syntax instead.

Common examples in Bash and PowerShell:
• -eq — equal to
• -ne — not equal to
• -gt — greater than
• -ge — greater than or equal to
• -lt — less than
• -le — less than or equal to

Example: 1 -ge 2 outputs false (equivalent to 1 >= 2).

⚠️ In Bash, symbolic operators like > mean redirection, not comparison — that's exactly why Bash uses -gt instead. Writing [ $var > 5 ] in Bash will silently redirect output to a file named "5" instead of comparing values.

front:
🎯 An analyst needs to run a script that parses an Apache access log for source IPs generating more than 100 requests per minute. The target system is an Ubuntu server. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate scripting language choice?

A) PowerShell
B) Bash
C) Visual Basic
D) C++
back:
✅ B) Bash

Bash is the default shell on Ubuntu and most Linux distributions — it has direct access to Linux command-line tools (awk, sort, uniq, grep) that make log parsing trivial with pipes.

❌ Why not the others:
• PowerShell — Windows-native. Cross-platform PowerShell exists, but on a Linux target Bash is the idiomatic choice.
• Visual Basic — Windows/Office scripting, not a Linux log-parsing tool.
• C++ — a compiled language, not a scripting language. Requires a compile step, no shell integration.

💡 Python would also be a strong answer for cross-platform work — but among the four options, Bash is best for on-box Linux log parsing.

front:
🎯 An analyst needs to script bulk changes to Active Directory user attributes on a Windows Server domain controller. Which scripting language is MOST appropriate?

A) Bash
B) PowerShell
C) Python
D) YAML
back:
✅ B) PowerShell

PowerShell is the native Windows scripting language and has first-class support for Active Directory via the ActiveDirectory module (Get-ADUser, Set-ADUser, New-ADUser, etc.). It uses the same object model as .NET, so AD objects flow through the pipeline naturally.

❌ Why not the others:
• Bash — Linux-native. Can be installed on Windows (WSL, Git Bash), but has no native AD cmdlets.
• Python — cross-platform and capable via libraries like pyad or LDAP modules, but requires more setup and is not the idiomatic choice for on-box Windows admin work.
• YAML — a data serialization format, not a scripting language. You cannot execute YAML.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: On Windows targets, PowerShell is also the primary language for both defensive scripting AND for attacker post-exploitation (Empire, PowerSploit) — reading PowerShell fluently is essential for IR.

front:
🔍 An analyst reviews the following script snippet. What language is it, and how do you know?

var=1
if [ "$var" -gt 1 ]; then
    echo "$var is greater than 1!"
else
    echo "$var is less than or equal to 1!"
fi
back:
Bash.

Tells:
• $var reference syntax with $ only on retrieval (not assignment) — Bash style. PowerShell would use $var in both assignment and retrieval.
• Square brackets [ ... ] around the condition — Bash test syntax.
• Letter-based operator -gt — Bash comparison syntax.
• then keyword after the condition — Bash if syntax.
• fi to close the block — the definitive Bash tell.
• echo for output — used by Bash (and also PowerShell as an alias, but the other tells rule that out).

💡 Any one of fi, -gt, or then alone would be strong evidence — three together is conclusive.

front:
🔍 An analyst reviews the following script snippet. What language is it, and what does it do?

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Carl")
back:
Python. It defines a function greet that takes a name parameter and prints Hello, Carl!.

Tells:
• def keyword to define a function — Python-specific
• Colon ending the function-signature line — Python syntax
• Indentation-based block (no braces, no end) — Python's hallmark
• f"Hello, {name}!" — Python f-string syntax for string interpolation
• print() as a function with parentheses — Python 3 syntax

front:
🔍 An analyst reviews the following script snippet. What language is it, and how do you know?

$myVariable = 10
Write-Output "The value is $myVariable"
back:
PowerShell.

Tells:
• $ used in variable assignment ($myVariable = 10) — PowerShell convention. Bash uses no $ on assignment (myVariable=10) — the $ appears only when retrieving the value.
• Write-Output cmdlet with hyphenated Verb-Noun naming — PowerShell's cmdlet naming standard
• Double quotes with in-string variable expansion — supported in PowerShell (also Bash, but the cmdlet name is decisive)

⚠️ Bash would write this as myVariable=10 (no $, no spaces around =) followed by echo "The value is $myVariable".

front: 📝 What does the shebang line #!/bin/bash at the top of a script accomplish?
back:
The shebang (or "hashbang") tells the operating system which interpreter to use to execute the script. #!/bin/bash specifies that the file should be run by the Bash shell at /bin/bash.

💡 Notes:
• Only valid at the very first line of the file
• Common alternatives:
  • #!/usr/bin/env python3 — run with Python 3 from the user's PATH
  • #!/bin/sh — run with the POSIX shell
• Without a shebang, execution behavior depends on how the script is invoked (e.g., bash script.sh ignores it anyway; ./script.sh relies on it).

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: When investigating a suspicious script on a Linux host, always check the shebang first — attackers sometimes use #!/bin/sh pointing to a modified interpreter, or embed the shebang in unexpected file types to abuse execution.

front: 🎯 An analyst is designing an automation script that will be called by a SOAR platform. The SOAR needs to know whether the script succeeded or failed so it can decide whether to run the next step. What script feature enables this?
back:
✅ Exit codes (a.k.a. exit status).

The script sets a specific exit code (typically 0 for success, non-zero for failure) via an exit statement. The SOAR platform reads the exit code and branches accordingly in the playbook.

💡 Best practice for SOAR-integrated scripts:
• Use exit 0 for clean success
• Use distinct non-zero codes for different failure modes (e.g., exit 1 for network error, exit 2 for invalid input) — lets the playbook take different actions per failure type
• Combine with stderr messages for human-readable diagnostics

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: This is exactly the pattern that makes SOAR playbooks reliable — a script that silently swallows failures breaks the entire orchestration chain.

front: 📝 In the Bash line if [ -f "$filename" ]; then, what does the -f test do?
back:
-f is a Bash file test operator that returns true if the specified path exists AND is a regular file (not a directory, device, or symbolic link on its own).

💡 Related file-test operators worth knowing:
• -e — file/path exists (any type)
• -d — is a directory
• -r — is readable
• -w — is writable
• -x — is executable
• -s — file exists and is not empty

These enable defensive scripting — check that a file exists and is readable before trying to process it.

front:
🔍 An analyst sees this on the front of a Bash script:

chmod 888 file 2> /dev/null

Why is 888 guaranteed to fail, and what is 2> /dev/null doing?
back:
• Why 888 fails: chmod permissions are octal — each digit represents the read/write/execute bits for a user class (owner/group/other), with a maximum of 7 (rwx = 4+2+1). 8 is not a valid octal digit, so the command errors out.

• 2> /dev/null — redirects stderr (file descriptor 2) to /dev/null, the null device. This discards the default error message so it doesn't appear on-screen, letting the script provide its own custom error output via echo.

💡 File descriptors in Linux:
• 0 = stdin (standard input)
• 1 = stdout (standard output)
• 2 = stderr (standard error)

💡 Common variants:
• 2>&1 — redirect stderr to wherever stdout is going
• &> file — redirect both stdout and stderr to a file

front: 📝 What does the Python f"..." prefix on a string do?
back:
The f prefix creates an f-string (formatted string literal) — Python evaluates any expression inside curly braces {...} and inserts the result into the string.

Example:
name = "Carl"
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
# Output: Hello, Carl!

💡 Without the f, the string would print literally as Hello, {name}! — no variable expansion.

f-strings can also evaluate expressions:
• f"{2+2}" → 4
• f"{len(mylist)}" → prints the length of mylist

front:
🎯 An analyst is writing a Bash monitoring script that must run continuously and alert only when a specific log pattern appears. Which loop type is MOST appropriate?

A) for loop
B) while true loop
C) until loop that exits when the pattern appears
D) A single if statement
back:
✅ B) while true loop

A while true loop runs indefinitely — the condition is always true, so the loop keeps executing until externally interrupted or an internal break/exit triggers. This matches "run continuously and alert when a pattern appears."

❌ Why not the others:
• A) for loop — designed for a fixed number of iterations. Wrong for continuous monitoring.
• C) until loop that exits on match — would stop the moment the pattern appears; the analyst wanted alerts, not termination on first detection.
• D) Single if — evaluates once and exits. No repetition.

💡 In practice, alerting scripts pair while true with sleep N to avoid burning CPU, or use tail -f piped into a filter.

front: 📝 In an if...else chain, what happens if none of the conditions are true and there is no else clause?
back:
Nothing runs. The script skips the entire conditional block and continues to the next statement after it.

Example (Bash):
var=0
if [ $var -gt 1 ]; then
    echo "greater"
fi
# Nothing echoes. Script continues silently.

💡 This is often the intended behavior. But if you need to guarantee some path executes (e.g., logging a "no match" result), always include an else — silent no-ops are a common source of "why isn't my script logging anything" bugs.

front: 🌐 What are the two exam objectives covered by Lesson 11B (Scripting Languages)?
back:
• 1.3 — Given a scenario, use tools to determine malicious activity.
• 1.5 — Explain the importance of efficiency and process improvement in security operations.

💡 Cross-objective coverage is why this lesson touches on both reading/interpreting scripts (1.3) and using scripts to automate SOC processes (1.5) — the scripting language is the tool that spans both domains.

front: 📝 What is a shell script, and what are typical SOC/admin use cases?
back:
A shell script is a text file of commands executed by a shell interpreter (like Bash — Bourne Again SHell). Perfect for repetitive or complicated tasks; scales from a few commands to complex programming structures.

Common use cases:
• Creating backups
• Automating software updates and installations
• System maintenance
• Log parsing — locating important information stored in logs
• Chaining command-line tools — e.g., use Nmap to find hosts with ports 80/443 open, then run additional collection steps, then save the results

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Log parsing and tool chaining are the two shell-script use cases that most directly appear in day-to-day SOC work.

front: 📝 What is a shell command processor (a.k.a. shell type), and what are the two modes it operates in?
back:
The shell command processor is the program that provides the interface between the user and the operating system. Its role is to interpret and execute commands typed at a prompt or included in a script.

Two operating modes:
• Interactive mode — commands are typed in one at a time and executed immediately
• Script mode — commands are read from a file and executed in order

💡 The same shell can do both. When you type at a Bash prompt, you're in interactive mode; when you run ./backup.sh, you're invoking Bash in script mode.

front:
📝 Match each shell command processor to its distinguishing description:

A) ksh   B) sh   C) csh   D) tcsh   E) bash   F) zsh
back:
• A) Korn Shell (ksh) — proprietary UNIX systems, e.g., IBM AIX
• B) Bourne Shell (sh) — simple, lightweight; found on most *nix systems and devices
• C) C Shell (csh) — associated with proprietary UNIX, e.g., Oracle Solaris
• D) TENEX C Shell (tcsh) — improved version of C Shell; cross-platform
• E) Bourne Again Shell (bash) — improved sh; very widely used
• F) Z Shell (zsh) — expands upon Bash; supports many plugins (e.g., Oh My Zsh)

💡 Mnemonic for order of appearance in most shops: sh → ksh → csh → tcsh → bash → zsh (each mostly building on or reacting to earlier ones).

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: On a compromised system, check which shell an attacker used (/etc/passwd shows each user's login shell). A user account suddenly changed from /bin/nologin to /bin/bash is a red flag.

front: 📝 Which shell is described as an improved version of sh and is very widely used on Linux systems?
back:
Bourne Again Shell (bash).

• Named as a pun on the earlier Bourne Shell (Stephen Bourne)
• Default login shell on most Linux distributions (macOS switched to zsh as default in Catalina)
• Superset of sh — scripts written for sh generally run under bash, but not vice versa

front: 📝 Which shell is described as simple and lightweight, found on most *nix systems and devices — often used in embedded systems?
back:
Bourne Shell (sh).

• Created by Stephen Bourne at Bell Labs
• Foundational shell — many later shells (bash, ksh, zsh) build on its syntax
• Common on embedded devices and minimal Linux images because of its small footprint

front: 📝 Which shell expands upon Bash and supports many plugins (e.g., Oh My Zsh) to broaden its functionality?
back:
Z Shell (zsh).

• Default shell on macOS since Catalina (2019)
• Rich plugin ecosystem (Oh My Zsh framework)
• Adds features like advanced tab completion, spelling correction, and themed prompts

front: 📝 What is the sh-bang (shebang) line, and what does #!/bin/bash specify?
back:
The shebang is the first line of a shell script that specifies which interpreter should be used to run the script. Format: #!/path/to/interpreter.

Common examples:
• #!/bin/bash — run with Bash
• #!/bin/sh — run with the Bourne Shell (POSIX)
• #!/usr/bin/env python3 — run with Python 3, using the user's PATH to locate it (portable)

⚠️ Must be the very first line of the file to be recognized.

front: 📝 What are the two commands needed to make a shell script executable and then run it in Bash?
back:
1. Make it executable:
    chmod +x scriptname.sh

2. Run it from the command line:
    ./scriptname.sh

💡 The ./ tells Bash to look for the script in the current directory — required because the current directory is not on PATH by default (a security convention that prevents accidentally running malicious files planted in your working directory).

front:
📝 Match each Linux command to its purpose:

A) cat
B) tail
C) head
D) touch
E) mkdir
back:
A) cat — displays file contents
B) tail — displays the last 10 lines of a file
C) head — displays the first 10 lines of a file
D) touch — creates an empty file (or updates timestamp)
E) mkdir — creates a directory

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: tail -f /var/log/auth.log (follow mode) is the workhorse for live log monitoring. Pair with grep to filter in real time.

front:
📝 Match each Linux command to its purpose:

A) cp
B) mv
C) rm
D) file
E) ls
back:
A) cp — copies a file or directory
B) mv — moves and renames files and directories
C) rm — removes a file or directory
D) file — determines the file type (by reading magic bytes, not by extension)
E) ls — lists the contents of a directory

💡 file is a malware triage staple — it reveals whether a suspicious ".jpg" is really an ELF executable or PE file with a swapped extension. Attackers rely on users trusting extensions; file defeats that trust.

front: 🔍 Distinguish locate from find. Which is faster, and why?
back:
• locate — searches for files using a prebuilt database (typically mlocate or plocate) that's updated periodically (usually daily via cron). Fast because it doesn't scan the filesystem at query time.

• find — searches by parsing the file system live at each invocation. Slower but always current and supports rich filter expressions (name, size, modification time, permissions, ownership).

⚠️ Locate can miss recently created files if the database hasn't been updated (sudo updatedb refreshes it).

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: For IR, use find — the database locate queries could be tampered with or stale, and attackers routinely drop files between database refreshes.

front: 🌐 Distinguish wget from curl. Both retrieve content from an HTTP server — when is each preferred?
back:
• wget — simpler, download-oriented; recursive downloads (mirror a whole site), automatic retries, resume interrupted downloads. Made for "grab this file (or these files) and save to disk."

• curl — more sophisticated options; supports many protocols (HTTP/HTTPS/FTP/SFTP/SMTP, etc.), custom headers, POST/PUT/DELETE, cookies, authentication. Made for "interact with any endpoint programmatically."

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Both are heavily abused by attackers for payload staging — after initial code execution, malware often calls curl or wget to download the next-stage binary. Seeing either in an unusual process tree (e.g., invoked by a web-server process) is a strong post-exploitation indicator.

front:
📝 Match each administrative Linux command to its purpose:

A) vi / vim
B) su
C) sudo
D) useradd
E) usermod
back:
A) vi / vim — opens a file editor in the terminal (very popular, not intuitive)
B) su — substitutes (switches) users. su - becomes root by default.
C) sudo — elevates privileges for the following command that requires higher access. Logs the invocation.
D) useradd — creates a user account
E) usermod — changes attributes of an existing user account (add to group, change shell, etc.)

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: These commands should be under audit. Alert on useradd, usermod -aG sudo, and unusual su/sudo patterns — attackers use them to establish persistence and privilege after initial access.

front: 🔍 Distinguish su from sudo. Which does a SOC prefer to see used, and why?
back:
• su (substitute user) — opens a new shell as another user. Requires that user's password. Once running, every command in the resulting shell is that user (no per-command audit context).

• sudo (superuser do) — runs a single command as another user (typically root). Requires the invoking user's own password. Every use is logged to /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure.

✅ SOC preference: sudo — per-command audit trail, least-privilege granularity, and no shared root passwords.

⚠️ sudo su - defeats the audit benefit by opening an unlogged root shell after the sudo. Attackers love this pattern; audit rules should flag it.

front: 📝 Distinguish chmod from chown.
back:
• chmod (change mode) — determines who is allowed to make changes to a file/folder — i.e., sets read/write/execute permissions for owner, group, and others.

• chown (change owner) — determines who owns a file/folder — sets the file's owning user and group.

💡 Order of operations after a suspicious change:
1. ls -la — check current owner and permissions
2. stat filename — get detailed metadata including modification timestamps

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Attackers frequently use chmod +s to make binaries SUID-root — a common privilege-escalation persistence technique. Flag any non-standard SUID binaries during IR.

front: 📝 What is mkfifo, and what does FIFO stand for?
back:
mkfifo creates a special file called a pipe — a FIFO (First In, First Out) — that allows the output of one command to be passed to another.

💡 Unlike an anonymous shell pipe (|) that exists only for the duration of a single command line, a FIFO persists as a file on disk and can be read from and written to by separate processes at different times.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Attackers use named pipes for stealthy inter-process communication in some malware families — the pipe file often has an innocuous name in /tmp. Investigating /tmp for FIFO files (file reports "fifo (named pipe)") is a good IR practice.

front: 📝 What is the Bash syntax for assigning a variable, and how do you then reference it?
back:
Assignment — variable name, equal sign with NO spaces around it, then the value:
name=Carl

Reference — dollar sign followed by the variable name:
echo $name

⚠️ Common trap: spaces around = break Bash assignment. name = Carl is interpreted as running the command name with the arguments = and Carl — not as an assignment.

💡 Contrast with PowerShell, which requires spaces around the =.

front: 📝 Are variables in Bash case-sensitive?
back:
✅ Yes — variables in Bash are case-sensitive.

• name, Name, and NAME are three different variables
• By convention, environment variables are typically UPPERCASE ($PATH, $HOME, $USER) while local variables use lowercase

⚠️ This distinguishes Bash from PowerShell — PowerShell variables are NOT case-sensitive. Watch for this on cross-language questions.

front: 📝 What are the two Bash function syntaxes, and how do you pass arguments to a Bash function?
back:
Method 1 — with the function keyword:
function my_func() {
    code...
}

Method 2 — without the keyword (C-style):
my_func() {
    code...
}

Both use curly braces around the body. The parentheses are required but empty — you do NOT put arguments inside the parentheses in Bash.

Instead, arguments are passed at the call site, like a command-line invocation:
my_func arg1 arg2
Inside the function, arguments are accessed as positional parameters: $1, $2, $@ (all args), $# (arg count).

front: 📝 What is the until loop unique to Bash, and how does it differ from a while loop?
back:
The until loop executes code when the control expression is FALSE. It's the mirror image of a while loop (which runs while the expression is true).

• while [ cond ] — run while cond is true; exit when it becomes false
• until [ cond ] — run while cond is false; exit when it becomes true

💡 Both loops always execute the body zero or more times — they check the condition before the first iteration.

front:
📝 What does this Bash until loop do?

var=1
until [ $var -ge 5 ]; do
    echo "The current number is $var."
    ((var++))
done
back:
Prints "The current number is 1." through "The current number is 4.", then exits.

How it works:
• Condition: $var -ge 5 (is $var greater-than-or-equal to 5?)
• The loop runs while the condition is false — i.e., while $var < 5
• When $var reaches 5, the condition becomes true → loop breaks out
• ((var++)) is the iterator, incrementing each pass

⚠️ Note the output stops at 4, not 5 — the condition -ge 5 is checked at the start of each iteration, so once var becomes 5, the loop exits before the echo.

front: 📝 What is the basic syntax of a Bash until loop?
back:
until [ <condition to be evaluated> ]; do
    <code to execute while condition is false>
done

Key keywords:
• do — starts the loop body
• done — ends the loop

💡 Same do...done pattern as while and for loops in Bash.

front: 📝 Name the four Bash arithmetic operators and the four Boolean operators.
back:
Arithmetic operators:
• + Addition
• - Subtraction
• * Multiplication
• / Division

Boolean (logical) operators:
• && Logical AND (this AND that)
• || Logical OR (this OR that)
• ! Logical NOT (NOT this)

💡 In Bash, && and || also do short-circuit command chaining at the shell level:
• cmd1 && cmd2 — run cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeds (exit 0)
• cmd1 || cmd2 — run cmd2 only if cmd1 fails

front: 📝 What are the six Bash comparison operators that CertMaster labels as "String operators"?
back:
• -eq Equal to
• -ne Not equal to
• -gt Greater than
• -ge Greater than or equal to
• -lt Less than
• -le Less than or equal to

⚠️ Terminology note: CertMaster labels these as "String operators" — but they are actually numeric (integer) comparison operators in Bash. Bash's real string operators are =, !=, <, and > inside [ ]. For the exam, memorize what CertMaster calls them but understand what they actually do — [ "abc" -eq "abc" ] will throw an integer-expected error.

💡 Mnemonic — the letters are the abbreviations: equal, not equal, greater than, greater or equal, less than, less or equal.

front: 📝 What does the Bash =~ operator do?
back:
=~ — pattern matching of regular expressions against a given value or string.

Example (must use [[ ]] not [ ]):
if [[ $var =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    echo "$var is all digits"
fi

💡 This makes Bash capable of lightweight regex matching without shelling out to grep, useful for input validation in scripts.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Detection scripts often use =~ to test whether captured strings match IoC patterns (IP addresses, hash formats, URL schemes) before triggering alerts.

front: 📝 What is PowerShell, and what platform is it built on?
back:
PowerShell is a scripting language and shell for Microsoft Windows that is built on the .NET Framework. It has been the default shell since Windows 10.

PowerShell offers much greater functionality than the traditional Windows Command Prompt (cmd.exe) and supports a wide variety of programming elements — .NET types, object pipelines, and rich remoting.

💡 Notes worth knowing:
• PowerShell Core (v6+) / PowerShell 7 is cross-platform (runs on Linux and macOS too) — the platform lock-in to Windows is Windows PowerShell 5.1 and earlier
• Everything in the pipeline is an object, not a text stream (major difference from Bash)

front: 📝 What is the file extension for a PowerShell script, and how do you run one from the PowerShell prompt?
back:
• Extension: .ps1
• Run from prompt: navigate to the script location, then type:
    .\[scriptname].ps1

⚠️ On Windows, you may need to adjust execution policies with Set-ExecutionPolicy to permit scripts to run.

💡 The .\ prefix is analogous to Linux ./ — it forces PowerShell to look in the current directory.

front: 📝 What does Set-ExecutionPolicy do, and why does it exist?
back:
Set-ExecutionPolicy is the PowerShell cmdlet that adjusts the execution policy — a safety feature that controls which PowerShell scripts are permitted to run on a system.

Common values:
• Restricted — no scripts run (default on desktop Windows)
• RemoteSigned — local scripts run; downloaded scripts must be signed
• AllSigned — only signed scripts run, local or remote
• Unrestricted — all scripts run (prompts for downloaded)
• Bypass — no restrictions or prompts

⚠️ Execution policy is NOT a security boundary per Microsoft — it's trivially bypassed (powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File script.ps1). Attackers routinely use -ExecutionPolicy Bypass in their initial-access payloads.

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Detect -ExecutionPolicy Bypass in process command lines — it's a strong indicator of malicious PowerShell activity.

front: 📝 What is a cmdlet, and what naming convention do cmdlets use?
back:
A cmdlet (pronounced "command-let") is a specialized .NET command that interfaces with PowerShell. Each cmdlet is a compiled library that exposes a configuration or administrative task (e.g., starting a VM in Hyper-V).

Naming convention: Verb-Noun.

Examples:
• Set-Date — set the system date
• Get-ChildItem — list files/folders
• Write-Host — print to the PowerShell console
• Clear-EventLog — clear a Windows event log
• Get-Process — list running processes

💡 Approved verbs are drawn from a defined list (Get-Verb lists them). This makes cmdlet names highly predictable — knowing the noun lets you often guess the verb.

front:
📝 What does this PowerShell script do?

Write-Host "Clearing event log..."
Clear-EventLog -logname Security, Application -computername Server01
Write-Host "Event log cleared!"
back:
Prints a status message, clears both the Security and Application event logs from the remote system Server01, and then prints a completion message.

Cmdlet breakdown:
• Write-Host — prints the given text to the PowerShell window
• Clear-EventLog — clears the specified logs
  • -logname Security, Application — comma-separated list of logs to clear
  • -computername Server01 — target host

🚨 Critical IR context: Clear-EventLog is a textbook attacker anti-forensics technique (mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1070.001 — Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs). Any use of it, especially on remote servers, should generate a high-severity alert.

💡 Event ID 1102 (Security log cleared) is itself logged and cannot be suppressed — so even when attackers clear logs, this event proves it happened.

front: 📝 What is the syntax for assigning a PowerShell variable, and how do you reference it?
back:
Assignment — all PowerShell variables begin with $; use = with spaces on either side; string values in quotes:
$name = "Carl"

Reference — call the variable by its name (with $):
Write-Output "My name is $name"
# Output: My name is Carl

⚠️ Two contrasts with Bash:
• PowerShell uses $ on both assignment and reference. Bash uses it on reference only.
• PowerShell requires spaces around =. Bash forbids them.

front: 📝 Are variables in PowerShell case-sensitive?
back:
❌ No — PowerShell variable names are NOT case-sensitive.

$name, $Name, and $NAME all refer to the same variable.

⚠️ This is a high-value distinction:
• Bash variables — case-sensitive
• PowerShell variables — case-INsensitive
• Python variables — case-sensitive

💡 The exam will test this distinction. Two of three case-sensitive, PowerShell is the odd one out.

front: 📝 What is the PowerShell syntax for declaring an array?
back:
Array subexpression operator @() with items separated by commas:
$my_array = @("Kai", "Ali", "Joseph")

Arrays are indexed from zero:
• $my_array[0] → "Kai"
• $my_array[1] → "Ali"
• $my_array[2] → "Joseph"

Modify elements by referencing their index: $my_array[1] = "Ari".

💡 Alternative syntax — the comma operator alone also creates an array:
$my_array = "Kai", "Ali", "Joseph"

front: 📛 CertMaster (Module 11 Lesson 11B) contains a contradictory statement in the PowerShell Arrays section. What is it, and what should you know for the exam?
back:
📛 Defective source explanation

The CertMaster text says (paraphrased):
"To declare an array in PowerShell, use the @() syntax with a comma to separate each item. For example: $my_array = @("Kai", "Ali", "Joseph"). Arrays are indexed from zero, so $myArray[0] is 1, $myArray[1] is "Hello", and so on."

The bolded portion is a copy-paste error from the earlier Bash arrays section (which used the array my_arr=(1 "Hello" 3.1)). It contradicts the immediately-preceding declaration.

Reality for the given declaration:
• $my_array[0] → "Kai"
• $my_array[1] → "Ali"
• $my_array[2] → "Joseph"

💡 The exam is unlikely to reproduce a copy-paste bug, but if you see a PowerShell array question with the values "Kai"/"Ali"/"Joseph", trust the declaration — not the follow-up sentence.

front:
📝 What does this PowerShell foreach loop do?

$myArray = @("Kai", "Ali", "Joseph")
foreach ($person in $myArray) {
    Write-Output "$person is a member of the team."
}
back:
Iterates over each element of $myArray, printing:
Kai is a member of the team.
Ali is a member of the team.
Joseph is a member of the team.

Syntax notes:
• foreach ($person in $myArray) — $person is the iterator variable, assigned to each element in turn
• Curly braces { } delimit the loop body — { opens the block, } closes it
• Note this is different from PowerShell's ForEach-Object cmdlet (used in a pipeline as | ForEach-Object { }), though functionally similar for many cases

front: 📝 In PowerShell, what is the difference between single-quoted and double-quoted strings, and what does each produce given $name = "Carl"?
back:
• Single quotes (' ') — treated as a literal string. Variable expansion and escape characters are NOT processed.
echo 'My name is $name'
# Output: My name is $name

• Double quotes (" ") — allow variable expansion and escape characters.
echo "My name is $name"
# Output: My name is Carl

💡 This rule is identical to Bash. The exam expects you to apply it to both languages.

front: 📝 What is the PowerShell escape character, and how does it differ from Bash and Python?
back:
Backtick (`) is the PowerShell escape character.

Language comparison:
• PowerShell → backtick `
• Bash → backslash \
• Python → backslash \

⚠️ PowerShell is the odd one out — this is a common exam trap. The backtick in most other contexts (Bash, Markdown) means something entirely different (command substitution / inline code), so it's easy to forget PowerShell repurposes it.

💡 Also, in PowerShell the backtick is used for line continuation — placing a backtick at the end of a line means "the statement continues on the next line."

front: 📝 List several PowerShell metacharacters that require escaping when used as literal characters.
back:
PowerShell has a larger metacharacter set than Bash. Common ones:
• Space and tab keystrokes
• Backtick (`) — the escape char itself
• Dollar sign ($)
• Single and double quotes (' and ")
• Semicolon (;)   Pipe (|)   Ampersand (&)
• Comma (,)   At sign (@)
• Parentheses (( ))   Curly braces ({ })   Square brackets ([ ])   Angle brackets (< >)
• Exclamation (!)
• Arithmetic-style: =, +, -, *, /, %
• Question mark (?)

To escape any of these, prefix with the backtick: `$, `", etc.

front:
📝 What does this PowerShell script do, and what role does param() play?

function Greet {
    param ($name)
    Write-Output "Hello, $name"
}

Greet "Carl"
back:
Defines a function Greet that accepts one parameter ($name) and prints a greeting. Calling Greet "Carl" outputs: Hello, Carl

Syntax notes:
• function — keyword that starts the definition
• Greet — the function name
• param($name) — declares the parameter(s) the function accepts. Placed inside the function body (unlike languages where parameters go in the function signature's parentheses)
• Curly braces delimit the body

💡 Cross-language function-definition contrast:
• PowerShell → function name { param(...); ... }
• Python → def name(param1, param2):
• Bash → name() { ... } (no parameters in parens; use $1, $2, ...)

front: 📝 Name the five common PowerShell loop types and give a one-line description of each.
back:
1. foreach — iterates over each item in a collection
2. for — loops a specific number of times (C-style: init; condition; iterator)
3. while — continues as long as a condition is true (checked before each iteration)
4. do-while — repeats while a condition is true, but the body always runs at least once (condition checked after)
5. do-until — repeats until a condition becomes true (body runs at least once; opposite of do-while)

💡 Key do-while/do-until distinction — the condition is checked at the end, so the body always executes at least once. In contrast, while checks the condition first and may skip the body entirely.

front: 🔍 What is the difference between PowerShell while and do-while?
back:
• while — checks the condition BEFORE the first iteration. If the condition is false at the start, the body never runs.

• do-while — checks the condition AFTER each iteration. The body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false from the start.

Syntax:
• while ($cond) { ... }
• do { ... } while ($cond)

💡 Use do-while when you need to execute a request at least once and possibly retry — e.g., prompt the user for input, then re-prompt if invalid.

front: 📝 Name the five PowerShell arithmetic operators. Which one does Bash lack?
back:
• + Addition
• - Subtraction
• * Multiplication
• / Division
• % Modulus (remainder)

The % modulus operator is the one CertMaster's Bash operator list does not include. (Bash can still do modulus with $((a % b)), but it's not in CertMaster's Bash operator table.)

💡 Modulus returns the remainder of a division:
• 7 % 3 → 1
• 10 % 5 → 0
• Commonly used to test even/odd: if ($n % 2 -eq 0)

front: 📝 Name the six PowerShell comparison operators and the three Boolean operators.
back:
Comparison operators (letter-based, like Bash):
• -eq Equal to    • -ne Not equal
• -gt Greater than    • -ge Greater or equal
• -lt Less than    • -le Less or equal

Boolean (logical) operators:
• -and Logical AND
• -or Logical OR
• -not or ! Logical NOT

⚠️ Bash vs PowerShell Boolean syntax is the classic trap:
• Bash: &&, ||, !
• PowerShell: -and, -or, -not (or !)
Both use letter-based comparison operators (-eq, etc.), but the Boolean operator style diverges.

front:
📝 What do these PowerShell string/pattern operators do?

A) -like
B) -match
C) -replace
D) + (on strings)
back:
A) -like — wildcard pattern matching (uses * and ?). Also -notlike.
  • "filename.log" -like "*.log" → $true

B) -match — regular expression pattern matching. Also -notmatch.
  • "user123" -match "^user\d+$" → $true

C) -replace — replaces matching text with a new value (regex).
  • "Hello World" -replace "World", "PowerShell" → "Hello PowerShell"

D) + (on strings) — string concatenation.
  • "Hello" + " World" → "Hello World"

⚠️ -like vs -match is a high-value distinction: wildcards vs regex. Wildcards are simpler and safer for filenames; regex is more powerful but easy to write incorrectly.

front:
📝 What do these PowerShell "other" operators do?

A) ..
B) ,
C) +=, -=, *=, /=
back:
A) .. Range operator — creates a sequence of numbers.
  • 1..5 → 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
  • Useful in for/foreach loops: foreach ($i in 1..10) { ... }

B) , Array creation separator — creates an array without needing @().
  • $array = 1, 2, 3

C) Compound assignments — apply an operation and reassign in one step.
  • $x += 5 is shorthand for $x = $x + 5
  • Same pattern for -=, *=, /=

front: 📝 What is Python, and how does it fundamentally differ from Bash and PowerShell?
back:
Python is a popular interpreted, general-purpose programming language designed for high readability with simple, clean syntax. Commonly used for automation tools, security tools, malicious scripts, and teaching object-oriented programming (OOP).

Key differences from Bash and PowerShell:
• Python is NOT a command shell tied to an operating system — it's a standalone language
• Cross-platform interpreter with its own extensive library ecosystem
• "Interpreted" means the program runs inside an executable environment — Python is not compiled into a standalone executable itself; the interpreter must be activated to run scripts

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Python's cross-platform nature makes it the go-to for security tooling — a single Python script can run on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Metasploit modules, threat intel enrichment scripts, and forensics tools are overwhelmingly Python.

front: 📝 Name the four key concepts CertMaster identifies as fundamental to Python.
back:
1. Spaces (whitespace) — Python's syntax is built around indentation. Blocks of code are initiated and terminated with indentation, rather than the curly braces { } used in Java/PowerShell/C.

2. Capitalization — Python is case-sensitive. user, User, and USER are three different names.

3. Comments — marked by the # character; anything after # on that line is ignored by the interpreter.

4. Help — inline documentation via the help() statement. E.g., help(print) displays help for the print function.

front: 📝 What is the current major version of Python, and why does Python 2 still matter?
back:
Current version: Python 3. Use it for any new work.

Why Python 2 still matters:
• Many legacy applications originally written in Python 2 remain in production
• Syntax differences (notably print as a statement in Python 2 vs. a function in Python 3) can break scripts if run against the wrong interpreter
• Some enterprise systems still ship with Python 2 pre-installed for backward compatibility

💡 Confirm the installed version with:
python3 --version

⚠️ Python 2 reached end of life in January 2020 — it receives no more official patches. Discovering Python 2 in production is a security finding worth flagging in itself.

front: 📝 What commands install Python 3, plus common supporting tools, on Ubuntu vs Red Hat–derived distributions?
back:
Ubuntu / Debian-derived:
apt update
apt install python3
apt install python3-dev
apt install python3-pip

Red Hat–derived (RHEL/Fedora/Rocky):
dnf install python3
dnf install python3-devel
dnf install python3-pip

Package roles:
• python3 — the interpreter itself
• python3-dev / python3-devel — headers/libraries for building Python C extensions
• python3-pip — the Pip package manager

💡 Most modern Linux distros include Python 3 by default; these commands are for confirming presence or adding supporting tooling.

front: 📝 What is the file extension for a Python script, and how do you run one on Windows vs Linux?
back:
Extension: .py

Windows:
  python myscript.py
  Or if multiple versions are installed: python3 myscript.py

Linux:
  python3 ./myscript.py
  The ./ tells Linux to look in the current directory.

front: 🔐 Why does Linux require the ./ prefix when running a script in your home directory, and what is the security reason for this?
back:
The PATH environment variable defines where the shell looks for executable commands. Your home directory is NOT on PATH by default — so Bash won't find scripts there without the ./ prefix.

To run a program in a location not on PATH, you must precede it with ./ to force the shell to check the current directory.

🔐 Security reason: Never add the home directory (or, more famously, . — the current directory) to PATH. If you did, an attacker who dropped a malicious binary named ls or sudo in a directory you cd into could get you to execute it instead of the real system binary.

💡 The Bash behavior of not auto-checking the current directory is a defense-in-depth measure against exactly this class of trojan-horse attacks.

front: 📝 What are the three steps to create and run hello.py as an executable in Linux?
back:
Step 1 — write the script with a shebang line as the first line:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
print("Hello World")

Step 2 — set the executable permission with chmod:
chmod +x hello.py

Step 3 — run the script (in the same directory):
python3 ./hello.py

💡 The shebang #!/usr/bin/env python3 is portable — it uses env to find python3 on the user's PATH, so the script works regardless of whether Python is installed at /usr/bin/python3, /usr/local/bin/python3, or a virtualenv location. Prefer this form over hard-coding #!/usr/bin/python3.

front: 📝 What is an IDE, and what four Python-friendly IDEs does CertMaster name?
back:
An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is a dedicated program for writing code, typically with:
• Editing environment with syntax highlighting
• Compiler or interpreter to compile and execute code
• Version control integration (e.g., Git)
• Support for multiple languages
• Extensibility via plugins
• (Some) AI capabilities for code analysis and optimization

Four IDEs for Python:
• IDLE — Python's built-in simple, user-friendly editor
• PyCharm — powerful IDE with many plugins, multi-language
• Visual Studio Code (VS Code) — Microsoft's flexible, lightweight, cross-platform editor
• Codium — the open-source alternative to VS Code with strong privacy features

💡 VS Code vs Codium — same underlying editor (open-source core), but VS Code binaries from Microsoft include telemetry and a proprietary marketplace license. Codium strips those out.

front: 📝 Distinguish Python modules, packages, and libraries.
back:
• Modules — collections of functions, classes, and variables in a single .py file. Imported to reuse code without rewriting it.

• Packages — collections of modules designed to work together. Identified by an __init__.py file in the project directory. Tracked centrally at the Python Package Index (PyPI) (nearly 600,000 projects).

• Libraries — bundles of related modules and packages. Typically contain collections of packages. Documentation often uses "library" and "package" interchangeably.

💡 Hierarchy: module ⊂ package ⊂ library. But in practice these boundaries are fuzzy — treat the terms as overlapping.

Python ships with the Python Standard Library (extensive default functionality) and users add other libraries via pip.

front:
📝 Match each built-in Python module to its purpose:

A) os
B) datetime
C) math
D) json
E) random
F) csv
back:
A) os — provides operating system interaction (file paths, env vars, spawning processes)
B) datetime — date and time manipulation
C) math — basic math functions (sqrt, sin, log, etc.)
D) json — interprets JSON-formatted data (parse and serialize)
E) random — random number generation
F) csv — interprets CSV-formatted data

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: For log parsing scripts, expect to see all of these — os for filesystem walking, datetime for timestamp conversion, json for structured logs (like Zeek or Wazuh output), and csv for exports/imports from ticketing systems.

front:
📝 Match each Python package/library to what it provides:

A) NumPy
B) pandas
C) PyGame
D) dateutil
E) pytest
back:
A) NumPy — technical and scientific features (arrays, linear algebra, numerical computing)
B) pandas — data manipulation (DataFrames — think spreadsheets in memory)
C) PyGame — video games and multimedia
D) dateutil — works with date and time information (parsing, timezone handling)
E) pytest — code testing framework

front:
📝 Match each additional Python library to what it provides:

A) matplotlib
B) PyTorch
C) Requests
back:
A) matplotlib — data visualization (plotting, charts, graphs)
B) PyTorch — computer vision and natural language processing (deep learning framework)
C) Requests — HTTP interactions (requests.get(), requests.post(), etc.)

🎯 SOC Analyst Perspective: Requests is the workhorse for querying REST APIs — threat intel feeds (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB), SIEM APIs (Splunk, Elastic), and SOAR webhooks. If you write Python for SecOps, you WILL use it.

front: 📝 What are dependencies in Python, and what is the purpose of a requirements.txt file?
back:
Dependencies are the modules, packages, and libraries a Python program requires to function.

requirements.txt — a text file documenting each dependency on an individual line, with optional version constraints.

Purposes:
• Lets other developers know what components the script/app uses
• Lets Pip install the appropriate resources automatically with one command:
  pip install -r requirements.txt
• Reproducible environments — the same requirements file gives everyone a consistent stack

💡 Best practice: store requirements.txt in the Python virtual environment for the project. Version-specific pinning avoids "works on my machine" bugs when a package updates and breaks compatibility.

front:
📝 Interpret this requirements.txt line:

numpy>=1.20 requests<=2.26
back:
This file indicates the program works with:
• Any NumPy version greater than or equal to 1.20
• Any Requests version less than or equal to 2.26

💡 Version specifier syntax:
• == — exact match (numpy==1.20.0)
• >= — at least this version
• <= — at most this version
• != — not this version
• No specifier — any version

⚠️ Very loose constraints (like numpy with no version) can lead to broken installs when a future release introduces breaking changes. Very tight constraints (==) can lead to unpatched-vulnerability situations. The lock-file pattern (e.g., Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock) helps balance these.

front:
📝 What is Pip, and what do each of these commands do?

A) pip install numpy
B) pip install numpy==2.2.0
C) pip show numpy
D) pip uninstall numpy
E) pip list
F) pip install -r requirements.txt
back:
Pip is the Python package manager for installing, updating, and removing packages, libraries, and modules.

Command breakdown:
A) Installs latest NumPy from PyPI
B) Installs the specific version 2.2.0 (version pinning)
C) Shows metadata about the installed NumPy package (version, location, dependencies)
D) Removes NumPy from the environment
E) Lists all installed packages and their versions
F) Installs every package specified in the requirements.txt file

💡 Create virtual environments for Python projects — python3 -m venv venv. Then activate and use pip inside the venv to keep project dependencies isolated. This prevents version conflicts across projects on the same system.

front: 📝 How do you assign a variable in Python, and what naming convention is typical?
back:
Assignment — variable name, = (with or without spaces — spaces are the convention), then value:
name = "Carl"

Reference — just the variable name:
print(name)
# Output: Carl

Naming convention:
• Variable names are case-sensitive
• Typically use snake_case — lowercase letters and underscores — for readability
• PEP 8 (the Python style guide) recommends this convention

💡 Cross-language variable syntax summary:
• Bash: name=Carl (no spaces, no $ on assign)
• PowerShell: $name = "Carl" (spaces required, $ always)
• Python: name = "Carl" (spaces conventional, no $)

front: 📝 In Python, what is the difference between single, double, and triple quotes for string literals?
back:
• Single quotes (' ') and double quotes (" ") — no functional difference. Either works; pick one and be consistent.

• Triple quotes (''' ''' or """ """) — required if you want line breaks in the string (multi-line strings). Also conventionally used for docstrings — function/class documentation.

Example:
msg = """Line one
Line two
Line three"""

⚠️ Contrast with Bash and PowerShell where single quotes are literal (no expansion) and double quotes allow variable expansion. In Python, that role is filled by f-strings, not by quote type.

front:
📝 What does this Python code output, and how does an f-string work?

name = "Carl"
message = f"Hello, {name}!"
print(message)
back:
Output: Hello, Carl!

F-strings (formatted string literals) let you embed variables and expressions directly into strings using curly braces { }.

Marked by the f prefix before the opening quote. Python evaluates any expression inside the braces at runtime and substitutes the result.

💡 F-strings can evaluate expressions, not just variables:
• f"{2 + 2}" → "4"
• f"{len(mylist)}" → the length of mylist
• f"{name.upper()}" → the name in uppercase

Without the f prefix, curly braces are literal characters and no substitution occurs.

front: 📝 What are the Python metacharacters, and what is the escape character?
back:
Python has fewer metacharacters than Bash or PowerShell. Special characters include:
• Period (.)   • Asterisk (*)   • Plus sign (+)
• Question mark (?)
• Square brackets ([ ])
• Curly braces ({ })
• Parentheses (( ))

Escape character: backslash (\) — same as Bash.

💡 Cross-language escape character summary:
• Bash → \ (backslash)
• PowerShell → ` (backtick — the outlier!)
• Python → \ (backslash)

Common Python escape sequences: \n (newline), \t (tab), \\ (literal backslash), \" (literal double quote).

front: 📝 What is Python's list (its primary array-like structure), and what is the syntax?
back:
Python uses lists as its primary array-like data structure. Lists are ordered collections of items defined using square brackets with comma-separated values:
names = ["Kai", "Ali", "Joseph"]

Items are accessed by their zero-based index:
• names[0] → "Kai"
• names[1] → "Ali"
• names[2] → "Joseph"

💡 Array syntax across languages:
• Bash: my_arr=(1 "Hello" 3.1) — parentheses, spaces
• PowerShell: $arr = @("Kai", "Ali") — @(), commas
• Python: names = ["Kai", "Ali"] — square brackets, commas

front:
📝 What does this Python for loop output?

myArray = ["Kai", "Ali", "Joseph"]
for person in myArray:
    print(f"{person} is a member of the team.")
back:
Output:
Kai is a member of the team.
Ali is a member of the team.
Joseph is a member of the team.

Python for loops iterate directly over each element of an iterable (list, tuple, dict, string, etc.). No index counter needed.

💡 If you also need the index, use enumerate():
for i, person in enumerate(myArray):
    print(f"{i}: {person}")

front:
📝 What does this Python function do, and what keyword defines it?

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}")

greet("Carl")
back:
Output: Hello, Carl

Functions in Python are defined with the def keyword, followed by the function name and any parameters in parentheses.

Structure:
• def → keyword
• greet → function name
• (name) → parameter list
• : → colon ending the signature
• Indented block → function body

front:
📝 What do these two Python loops do, and what determines the loop body in Python?

A) for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

B) count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1
back:
A) for loop with range(1, 6) — prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
• range(1, 6) generates numbers from 1 up to but not including 6.

B) while loop — prints 1 through 5.
• Condition count <= 5 is checked before each iteration.
• count += 1 is the iterator.

⚠️ Indentation identifies the body of the loop in Python — no curly braces, no done. The indented block ends when the indentation returns to the previous level.

💡 range() gotcha: the stop value is exclusive. range(1, 6) yields 1–5, not 1–6.

front: 📝 Name the seven Python arithmetic operators.
back:
• + Addition
• - Subtraction
